Theme: Neuroscience, Emotional Intelligence, Marriage Counselling and Islamic Spirituality

Why do couples who genuinely love each other repeatedly hurt one another? Why do small disagreements become major arguments? Why does one spouse pursue conversation while the other withdraws? And how can couples break destructive patterns and build a marriage characterised by emotional safety, mutual understanding and sakīnah?

In this insightful lecture, Ustaz Dr. Abdulfattah Adeyemi explores the fascinating intersection of neuroscience, psychology, marriage counselling and Islamic spirituality to help us understand what happens inside us—and between us—when relationships become emotionally challenging.

Our nervous systems influence how we respond to criticism, interpret silence, experience emotional triggers, and manage conflict. When we understand these responses, we can begin moving from automatic reactions towards deliberate, compassionate and responsible behaviour.

Drawing on practical relationship principles and the guidance of the Qur'an and Sunnah, this lecture offers a deeper understanding of what it takes to build a healthier, more peaceful and spiritually fulfilling marriage.

THIS LECTURE IS FOR:

Married couples seeking to improve communication and emotional intimacy.

Singles preparing for marriage and wanting to understand relationship dynamics.

Muslim couples interested in integrating Islamic values with practical relationship skills.

Parents, family counsellors, marriage educators and relationship coaches.

Anyone interested in emotional intelligence, human behaviour and personal development.

You may not control every emotion that arises within you, but you can learn to respond more wisely. A healthier marriage is not necessarily one without disagreements; it is one in which both partners learn to address difficulties with greater understanding, responsibility, respect and mercy.

recent_video_description:
Are Muslims sometimes making it harder for people to embrace Islam, practice their faith, or find a place within the Muslim community?

In **Season 7, Episode 6 of *Talking With Teachers***, Dr. Abdullah bin Hamid Ali welcomes **Dr. Shadee ElMasry**, founder of Safina Society, for a wide-ranging and thought-provoking conversation about Muslim identity, religious commitment, community leadership, and the importance of prophetic character.

Drawing on his upbringing in America, his experiences studying Islam in Morocco, and his years of teaching and community work, Dr. Shadee reflects on the challenges facing Muslims today—and what it means to build strong, principled, and compassionate Muslim communities.

**Among the questions explored:**

- Are Muslims sometimes too judgmental toward one another?
- How can we maintain Islamic principles without alienating people who are struggling?
- What responsibilities do American Muslims have toward their neighbors and wider society?
- Why is compassion essential to effective da'wah?
- What role do traditional scholarship, good character, and spiritual companionship play in preserving Islam for future generations?

The conversation also explores Muslim political engagement, the influence of converts on American Islam, the importance of community service, and the need to build lasting connections with Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and the Muslim community.

**One particularly challenging question emerges:** If Muslims disappeared from their communities tomorrow, would their neighbors notice their absence? Would they miss the contributions Muslims make to society?

This episode challenges us to consider not only how faithfully we practice Islam, but also how effectively we embody its teachings in our relationships with others.

**Watch the full conversation and share your thoughts:** How can Muslims uphold their religious principles while making their communities more welcoming, compassionate, and beneficial to society?

recent_video_title: Allah Will Not Look at Them
recent_video_description:
As I walk through the snowy woods I discuss those categories of people that  Allah will neither talk to nor look at, nor purify, and they will have a painful punishment. May Allah protect us. Ameen.

Indeed, they who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book and exchange it for a small price – those consume not into their bellies except the Fire. And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them. And they will have a painful punishment. [Qur’an 2:174]

Allah’s Messenger (ﷺ) said, “There are three persons whom Allah will neither talk to nor look at, nor purify from (the sins), and they will have a painful punishment. (They are): (1) A man possessed superfluous water on a way [some versions say ‘in a desert’] and he withheld it from the travelers. (2) a man who gives a pledge of allegiance to a Muslim ruler and gives it only for worldly gains. If the ruler gives him what he wants, he remains obedient to his pledge, otherwise he does not abide by it, and (3) a man bargains with another man after the `Asr prayer and the latter takes a false oath in the Name of Allah claiming that he has been offered so much for the thing and the former (believes him and) buys it.” (Bukhari)

In one version of the hadith, it adds the words:

فَيَقُولُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ، الْيَوْمَ أَمْنَعُكَ فَضْلِي، كَمَا مَنَعْتَ فَضْلَ مَا لَمْ تَعْمَلْ يَدَاكَ

Allah will say on the Day of Resurrection, ‘Today I withhold My Blessings from you as you withheld the superfluous part of that (water) which your hands did not create.’ (Bukhari)

Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) observed: “Three (are the persons) with whom Allah would neither speak, nor would He absolve them on the Day of Resurrection. Abu Mu’awiya added: He would not look at them and there is grievous torment for them: the aged adulterer, the liar king and the proud destitute.” (Muslim)

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “There are three at whom Allah will not look on the Day of Resurrection: The one who disobeys his parents, the woman who imitates men in her outward appearance, and the cuckold [husband of an adulterous wife]. And there are three who will not enter Paradise: The one who disobeys his parents, the drunkard, and the one who reminds people of what he has given them.” (Nasa’i)

recent_video_title: Dua - Weapon of the Believers
recent_video_description:
Public lecture delivered by Shaykh Yasir Qadhi titled 'Dua - The Weapon of the Believers' at the International Islamic Peace Conference 2009 held at Somaiya Ground Mumbai, India 2009, as shown on Peace TV.

International Islamic Peace Conference 2009 - Understanding Islam & Global Unity is a 10 Day International Islamic Conference & Exhibition that was held on 30th October to 8th November. The location a vast ground, Somaiya Ground (Spread over 30 acres) Sion (E), Mumbai, India. Admission is free: People of all religion were welcome.

Dua supplication) is the most powerful weapon of the believer and a means of communicating with his Lord - Shaykh Yasir Qadhi elaborates on the status, importance and etiquette of dua' in Islam. For more information and details please refer to the book published by the speaker of the same title which is the most comprehensive work yet to be written in English on the topic, the author discusses, amongst other matters: the excellence and benefits of du'a; the types of du'a; the pre-conditions that are needed in order for a du'a to be accepted; the recommended etiquette of performing du'a; the timings and situations in which a du'a is more likely to be answered; the various factors that aid or prevent a du'a from being accepted; the relationship of du'a with the Divine Decree (qadr); the wisdom behind a delayed response, and many other relevant topics.

Yasir Qadhi was born in Houston, Texas and completed his primary and secondary education in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. He graduated with a B.Sc. in Chemical Engineering from the University of Houston, after which he was accepted as a student at the Islamic University of Madinah. After completing a diploma in Arabic, he graduated with a B.A. from the College of Hadith and Islamic Sciences. Thereafter, he completed a M.A. in Islamic Theology from the College of Dawah.

His published works include Riya'a: The Hidden Shirk, Du'aa: The Weapon of the Believer, and An Introduction to the Sciences of the Qur'an.

recent_video_description:
Topic: This Is How You Make a Strong and Sincere Tawbah | 6 important Steps .
 Ustadh Abu Bakr Zoud 
Do you want to make a strong and sincere Tawbah (repentance) to Allah? ❤️

In this powerful Islamic reminder, discover the 6 essential steps to making a strong Tawbah to Allah (Subhanahu wa Ta'ala) and returning to Him with a sincere heart.

Here are the six important conditions of sincere repentance:

1. Tawbah for the sake of Allah: Turn back to Allah sincerely.
2. Fear, hope, and love: Repent out of fear of Allah, hope in His forgiveness, and love for Him.
3.Repent at the right time: Make Tawbah before the signs of the end of life arrive.
4.Regret your sins: Feel genuine remorse for what you have done.
5.Give up the sin: Stop committing the sin and turn back to Allah.6.
6. Make a firm commitment: Make a sincere intention in your heart never to return to that sin.
Remember, never lose hope in Allah's mercy. No matter how many mistakes you have made, turn back to Allah and seek His forgiveness.

May Allah grant us all sincere Tawbah and forgive our sins. Ameen. 🤲

recent_video_description:
Maulana Ismail Moosa (South Africa) faces Australian Reverend Samuel Green for the second time to unpack this fundamental question. IS THE CHRISTIAN CHRIST FOUND IN THE OLD TESTAMENT?

Christian View of Jesus in the Tanakh

Messianic Prophecies: Christians read the Tanakh as pointing forward to Jesus of Nazareth as the promised Messiah and Son of God. 
Passages like Isaiah 7:14 (the virgin birth), 
Isaiah 53 (the suffering servant), and 
Psalm 22 (details of the crucifixion) 
are interpreted as explicit previews of Jesus's life, death, and resurrection. The New Testament builds directly upon the Tanakh, viewing Jesus as the final and supreme word of God who fulfills the Law (Torah) and the Prophets (Nevi'im).

Islamic View of Jesus in the Tanakh

Islam views Jesus (Isa) as a Prophet, Messenger, and the Messiah (al-Masih) sent to the Children of Israel, rather than as God incarnate or the Son of God. Muslims respect the original revelations given to Moses (Taurat) and David (Zabur), which they believe originally pointed to pure Monotheism.
Islamic tradition holds that while the core message of past scriptures was divine, subsequent human interpretations or textual transmissions led Jews and Christians to misunderstand certain prophecies. Explore specific verses (such as Isaiah 7 or Psalm 110) to see how Christian and Islamic commentators interpret them differently?

Reverend Samuel Green—a Chemical Engineer and theologian—is no newcomer to interfaith dialogue. Having served as a campus evangelist and Islamic Engagement Director since 1999, as well as founding author of the Answering Islam website, he has debated almost every mainstream Muslim apologist over the last 15 years.

Positive Interpretations: Lessons from the Sahabah's Retreat

This video discusses a significant incident involving Abdullah ibn Umar (radiyallahu ta'ala anhuma) and Rasulullah (sallallahu alayhi wa sallam) that illustrates the principles of compassion and understanding in Islamic teachings. It highlights the following key points:

1. Greeting and Respect: When meeting someone regularly, a simple greeting (salaam) suffices. However, upon returning from a journey or meeting a pious or senior person, more affectionate gestures like embracing or kissing are encouraged.

2. Positive Interpretation of Actions: The document emphasizes the importance of interpreting actions positively, especially when someone makes a mistake. Instead of condemning or rebuking, one should look for a positive angle, as demonstrated by Rasulullah (sallallahu alayhi wa sallam) when he reframed the retreat of some Sahabah during a battle as a strategic regrouping rather than cowardice.

3. Encouragement Over Despair: Rasulullah (sallallahu alayhi wa sallam) provided encouragement to his followers, helping them learn from their setbacks rather than succumbing to despair. This approach fosters resilience and courage among believers.

4. Kissing the Hand of the Pious: The act of kissing the hand or forehead of a pious person is permissible and encouraged in Islam, as long as it is not done excessively. The document references a hadith where Abdullah ibn Umar and others expressed their reverence for the Prophet by kissing his hand.

Overall, the teachings promote a compassionate and understanding approach to interpersonal relations within the framework of Islamic principles.

recent_video_description:
How should Muslims understand the signs of Qiyamah? Is it correct to interpret current events as fulfilments of end-time prophecies?

In this insightful talk, Shaykh Akram Nadwi explains why the Prophet ﷺ informed us about the signs of the Day of Judgement, and why we should avoid speculating about their fulfilment. Using examples from the Qur'an and Sunnah, he discusses the meaning of ta'wil, the wisdom behind the signs of the Hour, and why only Allah knows when the Hour will come.

Rather than encouraging predictions, these signs are meant to strengthen our faith, inspire us to prepare for the Hereafter, and give believers hope in Allah's promise.

Topics covered:
• Why the Prophet ﷺ spoke about the signs of Qiyamah
• Should we link current events to end-time prophecies?
• The meaning of ta'wil
• The wisdom behind the signs of the Day of Judgement
• Why only Allah knows when the Hour will come

Want to learn more?

recent_video_title: Can Shaytan Use Your Good Deeds Against You? | Quranic Psychology | Dr Mohammad Akram Nadwi
recent_video_description:
What if Shaytan’s greatest trick is not always to make you sin—but sometimes to encourage you to do good?

In this powerful extract from the Who Am I? – Diploma in Qur’anic Psychology (Tazkiyah al-Nafs), Shaykh Dr Mohammad Akram Nadwi explores a subtle danger in the spiritual life: even prayer, fasting, teaching, charity and other acts of worship can become corrupted when the heart develops the wrong intention.

Drawing on the classical Islamic tradition, he explains three ways an apparently good deed can be corrupted:

1. Wrong intention — seeking admiration, status or superiority rather than Allah.
2. Wrong method — performing an act in a way that departs from the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ.
3. Wrong goal — using an act of worship primarily to obtain a worldly outcome for which it was not prescribed.

A person may outwardly be doing something virtuous while pride, self-admiration, showing off or the desire for worldly recognition quietly enters the heart.

The lesson is profound: tazkiyah is not simply about avoiding sins. It is about continually examining the heart—even while doing good.

From the Who Am I? – Diploma in Qur’anic Psychology with Shaykh Dr Mohammad Akram Nadwi at Cambridge Islamic College.

recent_video_title: Book Release: The Uncrucified Christ | Dr. Ali Ataie
recent_video_description:
The wait is over! Dr. Ali Ataie's highly anticipated book, The Uncrucified Christ, is officially here!

Was Jesus of Nazareth (ʿĪsā عليه السلام) actually crucified? Is the crucifixion an established historical fact, or is there room for a serious scholarly reassessment of one of the most widely accepted claims in Christian history?

In his groundbreaking new book, The Uncrucified Christ, Dr. Ali Ataie challenges conventional historical assumptions surrounding the crucifixion of Jesus and presents a scholarly defense of the historical plausibility of the Qur'anic account.

Drawing upon biblical scholarship, historical criticism, early Christian history, textual analysis, and Islamic theology, Dr. Ataie engages one of the most consequential questions in the history of Christian-Muslim dialogue: What really happened to Jesus of Nazareth?

The Qur'an declares:

"And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them." (Qur'an 4:157)

For centuries, the Qur'anic denial of Jesus' crucifixion has stood in sharp contrast to the traditional Christian narrative and the prevailing consensus among historians. But how conclusive is the historical evidence? What assumptions underlie the scholarly consensus, and can an alternative reconstruction of the events surrounding Jesus' final days be historically defensible?

What can the story of Umm Musa (the mother of Prophet Musa AS) teach us about tawakkul, worry, and trusting Allah’s plan?

Why did Allah test Umm Musa in this way? How evident was His mercy? How does Allah strengthen the human heart during uncertainty? And what does this story teach us about surrendering control while living in a world full of worry?

This session combines tafsir, spiritual reflection, and practical lessons to help us understand how the Qur’an speaks directly to our emotional and spiritual struggles today.

Topics covered:
 • The story of Um Musa in the Quran
 • Tawakkul (trust in Allah) explained through Qur’anic stories
 • Tadabbur: how to reflect deeply on the Qur’an

 this video, Shaykh Ammar shares a deeply personal and tragic story about the exact moment that led him to stop interpreting dreams.

This recording was delivered via the Muslim Community Center - East Bay (MCC East Bay) in Pleasanton, California on June 27, 2021.

We gather to mourn the victims of the horrific yearlong pandemic on our community.

The Coronavirus caused millions of deaths and disrupted billions of lives globally.

Group worship was also disrupted, but the outbreak has bolstered the religious faith of many faithful and opened opportunities to pray and to serve our community with food, medical supplies, and more.

Disasters and crises have a way of making some question the existence of a greater force for good in the world and others to become more religious in the wake of tragedy.

As we look forward to better days, we reflect on the intersection of faith, a pandemic, a historic social movement.

recent_video_title: Ep 142 - Is Your Halal Meat Really Halal? | The UK’s First Halal & Tayib Farm
recent_video_description:
What does halal truly require from us? Is it only about how an animal is slaughtered, or should it also include how that animal lived?

In this episode, Nadeem sits down with Khalil from Willowbrook Farm, the UK’s first Halal and Tayib farm, for a powerful conversation about food, farming, animal welfare, sustainability and our responsibility as Muslims toward the earth.

Khalil shares the remarkable Willowbrook story, beginning in 2002 when his parents left their careers, sold their home and committed themselves fully to building an ethical farm from empty land. The family faced years of opposition and planning difficulties, living in camouflaged caravans on their own land while raising thousands of chickens and working toward permission to build a permanent home.

The conversation explores why a halal stamp may tell us very little about the life an animal experienced. Khalil explains the difference between traditional chickens raised slowly over 12 weeks and commercial chickens produced in as little as four weeks, as well as the uncomfortable realities behind intensive, “free-range” and organic farming.

They also discuss:

• The difference between halal and Halal and Tayib
• Why cheap meat always carries a hidden cost
• Animal welfare before the moment of slaughter
• The problems with intensive and industrial farming
• Whether ethical farming can remain financially sustainable
• Foraging, mushrooms and reconnecting with nature
• Eating seasonally and using the whole animal
• Self-sufficiency and the limits of modern sustainable living
• Needs, wants and escaping consumer culture
• Repairing, reusing and delaying unnecessary purchases
• Islamic stewardship and our duty as caretakers of the earth
• Eco-camping, farm visits and activities at Willowbrook Farm

This is not simply a conversation about farming. It is an honest examination of the way we eat, consume and live, and whether our everyday choices reflect the values we claim to hold.

The goal is not perfection overnight. It is to become more conscious, eat less but eat better, ask where our food comes from and begin making small, meaningful changes.

recent_video_title: Moments with The Messenger | Episode 4: Beloved: The Women Who Raised the Prophet ﷺ
recent_video_description:
Beloved: The Women Who Raised the Prophet ﷺ

Seerah and Sisterhood: Love, Leadership, and Grief

In this gathering, we explore the women who nurtured the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the lasting place they held in his heart. Their stories invite us to reflect on caregiving, belonging, leadership, and loss—and to deepen our love for the Messenger ﷺ by getting to know him.

Our purpose is both Seerah and sisterhood: learning his story, applying its lessons, and building a community where women know and support one another.

In This Session

The women who nurtured him
We meet his mother, Aminah bint Wahb; his early wet nurse, Thuwaybah; his devoted caregiver, Barakah, known as Umm Ayman; and his wet nurse, Halimah al-Saʿdiyyah. Their care reminds us that the women who raise, nourish, and protect children have a lasting place in our collective story.

Milk kinship and the meaning of family
The discussion introduces milk kinship in Islam and the significance of bonds formed through nursing. These relationships carry enduring family connections and marriage restrictions, giving nursing a meaning far beyond a temporary arrangement of care.

Umm Ayman: a lifetime of love and service
Umm Ayman cared for the Prophet ﷺ from childhood, accompanied him through the loss of his mother, and remained beloved to him throughout his life. Her migration, service, and grief at the ending of revelation reveal a woman of profound faith whose story deserves to be remembered.

Zayd and Usamah: belonging, dignity, and leadership
The stories of Zayd ibn Harithah and his son, Usamah ibn Zayd, show how the Prophet ﷺ put human dignity into practice. His appointment of the young Usamah to lead an expedition challenged assumptions about age, ancestry, and social status.

Accountability with a path forward
Usamah’s story also brings together two powerful moments: the Prophet’s ﷺ strong correction of a grave mistake in battle and his later decision to entrust him with leadership. The lesson for parents, teachers, and community leaders is clear: hold young people accountable while allowing them to learn, grow, and earn trust.

Halimah and unexpected barakah
The session recounts the Seerah narrative of Halimah welcoming an orphan whom others had passed over, and the blessings her household experienced through his presence. Her story invites us to reconsider where we expect goodness to come from—and whom we might overlook.

Aminah’s love and the pain of letting go
Aminah’s decision to send her infant into another woman’s care opens a reflection on the difficult choices mothers make for their children’s well-being. The discussion follows his early childhood, the account of the opening of his chest, and his return to his mother.

A mother’s death and grief across a lifetime
The gathering closes with Aminah’s death when the Prophet ﷺ was six and his later tears at her grave. His enduring love reminds us that spiritual strength does not erase sorrow.

Lessons to Carry With Us

* Knowing the Prophet ﷺ deepens our love for him. Seerah invites us to internalize his example and bring it into our daily lives.
* Caregiving deserves recognition. The women who nurtured him remain part of the story we tell and honor.
* Equality becomes meaningful through decisions. Who we trust, appoint, and welcome reveals the values we live by.
* A serious mistake need not define a whole life. Correction and opportunities for growth belong together.
* Grief has no fixed timeline. Tears can coexist with patience, faith, and trust in Allah.
* Sisterhood requires mutual care. We become a community when we begin helping one another.

Reflect With a Sister

1. Who has nurtured you beyond your immediate family? How might you honor her?
2. Where might assumptions about age, race, or social standing shape whom you trust or recognize?
3. How can you hold someone accountable while leaving room for growth?
4. What does the Prophet’s ﷺ expression of grief give you permission to feel?
5. What is one step you can take this month to help turn this gathering into a community?

“Grief has no timeline. Grief is not negated by piety or sabr or tawakkul. Tears are rahma, and we follow a man who cried.”

The sacrifices that come with standing for what you believe in.

And the personal battles that the world never gets to see.

Where does conviction end and responsibility begin?

Because perhaps courage isn’t always about speaking louder.

But who we remain when the cameras are switched off, the applause fades and we are left alone with our conscience and Allah.

A conversation that goes beyond journalism, activism and public opinion.

A conversation about the experiences that shape us, the principles that guide us and the legacy we hope to leave behind.

recent_video_title: 11 Reasons Why Zakat is Easy
recent_video_description:
Paying Zakat doesn't have to be complicated. In this video, we'll show you why fulfilling this essential pillar of Islam is simpler than you think!

Here's what you'll discover:

✅ Designed for Simplicity: Zakat applies only to specific assets known as al-Mal al-Nami, assets acquired specifically for growth or exchange, including:
- Cash and monetary assets
- Trade goods
- Livestock meant for growth

✅ Clear Calculation: Following Imam Abu Hanifah’s view, Zakat is calculated at clear thresholds and brackets, simplifying the calculation process. Although, Hanafis do not practice on this view today, this was the opinion of Imam Abu Hanifah.

✅ Annual Obligation: Zakat is payable just once each year, after holding the assets for one complete lunar year.

✅ Profit-Based: Zakat is intended to be paid from your gains and profits, making it affordable and manageable.

✅ Debt-Friendly: Debts you owe can be deducted, reducing your overall Zakatable amount.

✅ Stable Calculation: Fluctuations in asset value throughout the year aren't considered, keeping calculations straightforward.

✅ Low Rate: Zakat is only 2.5% of your net Zakatable assets, making it affordable for everyone.

✅ Clear Ownership: You only pay Zakat on assets you fully own.

✅ Exemptions: Assets acquired without a clear intention for growth or exchange, and "weak" receivables, are exempt from Zakat.

CHAPTERS

You write down your feelings—but do your pages help you recognise progress and decide what to change?

In this video, Dr. Francesca Bocca-Aldaqre explores muḥāsaba: the Islamic practice of taking ourselves to account before Allah. She considers how reflection can move beyond recording thoughts and feelings toward examining our actions, recognising improvement, and making one clear decision for tomorrow.

This is the first video in our November series exploring five practices through the lens of Islamic Psychology: journaling, self-compassion, boundaries, thought-work, and meditation.

In this episode:
• The difference between journaling and muḥāsaba
• How reflection can turn into repetitive overthinking
• Why specific actions reveal more than harsh labels about ourselves
• How to recognise progress we may overlook

And ask yourself:
“Towards whom was my heart when I did it?”

💬 What is one small change you would like to make tomorrow? Share only what you feel comfortable sharing.

recent_video_title: The Screen and the Soul: Breaking Screen Addiction| Dr Francesca Bocca Aldaqre
recent_video_description:
Is your screen helping you rest—or helping you escape?

In Lecture 4, **The Screen and the Soul**, we explore screen addiction through the Islamic understanding of the nafs (self), qalb (heart), rūḥ (soul), and the work of tazkiyah: purification and spiritual growth.

From endless scrolling to the phone we reach for without thinking, this lecture examines how digital habits shape our attention, relationships, parenting, and connection with Allah. It asks us to look beneath the habit: what discomfort are we trying to avoid, and what would actually nourish us?

The central teaching is practical: removing a habit needs to be accompanied by cultivating something better. Reclaiming our attention begins with meaningful alternatives—Qur’an, dhikr, du‘ā, family connection, time outdoors, service, and purposeful activity.

IN THIS LECTURE:
• Dopamine, anticipation, and the pull of unpredictable rewards  
• Four patterns of screen dependence across different stages of life  
• Ghaflah (heedlessness), lahw (distraction), and hawā (unchecked desire)  
• The difference between numbing ourselves and finding restorative rest  
• Why app limits and willpower can leave underlying needs unresolved  
• Practical replacements for scrolling in the morning, during the commute, while waiting, and before sleep  
• How our digital habits shape the example we set for our children  
• Rebuilding our capacity to contribute to family and community  

CHAPTERS  
00:00 — Opening: The screen, the soul, and the possibility of change  
10:15 — Why screens? Why now?  
22:15 — Four faces of screen addiction, one underlying pattern  
35:35 — Training the nafs and cultivating better habits  
48:20 — Two practical assignments and closing du‘ā  

THIS WEEK’S PRACTICE  
Choose one daily moment when you automatically reach for your phone. Replace it with one specific practice for seven days: a page of Qur’an, a few minutes of dhikr, a du‘ā, or meaningful connection with someone you love.

You can also plan a day from Fajr to Maghrib with your phone put away. Decide beforehand what will fill that time: a walk, a family meal, a visit, reading, or an act of service.

REFLECTION  
What is one phone habit you want to change—and what will you put in its place? Share your intention in the comments.

ABOUT THE SERIES  
This is the fourth lecture in a five-part series exploring the inner life through an Islamic framework.

Next lecture: **The Entitled Child and the Exhausted Parent**

Subscribe for the next lecture, and share this reminder with someone who wants to reclaim their attention and strengthen their connection with Allah.

When someone insults us, hurts us or treats us unfairly, our natural reaction may be to retaliate. But the Quran teaches us something far more powerful: to respond to evil with what is best.

Allah says in Surat Fussilat (41:34):

“Good and evil are not equal. Repel evil with what is best, and the one between whom and you there was enmity will become as though he were a close friend.”

- What a worldview is, and why everyday phrases like “it’s my choice” are more loaded than they sound
- The wisdom framework: the righteous goal, the context, and applying knowledge in a way that fits, drawn from the example of the Prophet peace be upon him.

The deep taqwa and firm adherence to the sunnah and Shariah that characterized his teacher were eventually transferred to the student and Shaykh Husain was formally authorized in this science by Shaykh Zulfiqar (db) in July 2001.

Shaykh Husain has completed medical school and is currently an Assistant Professor of Pathology at University of Chicago's Prizker School of Medicine and also practices Surgical Pathology at the University of Chicago Medical Center. Pharaoh had just watched Musa (as) perform a miracle. He couldn’t deny what the people saw, so he did something more subtle and effective: he labeled it as magic. One word, and the proof became a trick, the messenger became a suspect, and the argument was already tilted before anyone weighed the evidence.

In this Snapshot, Imam Tom Facchine unpacks how that same move still works today, as language frames the moral universe before a debate begins, and why Muslim leaders must learn to recognize when a word or a question is a trap. Drawing on the Qur’an’s close attention to names, labels, and accusations, he shows what it looks like to answer without accepting someone else’s frame.

 — Why words like “extremism” and “moderation” aren’t neutral, and what they assume
 — Why some questions are built so that answering them means losing, and when a leader should reframe or refuse

The rise and reign of Marwan II (Marwan ibn Muhammad) marked the desperate final stand of the Umayyad Caliphate as internal fractures tore the empire apart from within. Emerging from years of rugged campaigning in the Caucasus, Marwan brought a hardened, regimental military doctrine to an empire paralyzed by systemic crisis and exhausted frontiers.   

The rapid collapse of central authority created an unprecedented power vacuum in the imperial core. Following the assassination of Walid II, the short caliphates of Yazid III and Ibrahim shattered dynasty legitimacy, sparking immediate challenges across Syria, Palestine, and Iraq. As royal contenders traded assassinations and purges, the volatile Qays-Yaman rivalry exploded into open civil war, disintegrating the traditional Syrian military dominance that had upheld the dynasty for nearly a century.   

Across the provinces, regional defiance accelerated the dynastic decline. The far western Maghreb splintered with the emergence of the heretical Bargawata Confederation, while the frontiers of Khorasan devolved into factional infighting between Nasr ibn Sayyar and Juday al-Kirmani. In Iraq, a sweeping Kharijite resurgence led by al-Dahhak overwhelmed major garrison towns, drawing defectors from every quarter.   

Marwan’s southern march from Haran culminated in the bloody Battle of Ain al-Jar, driving Ibrahim from power and placing Marwan on the throne of a fragmented realm. Yet even as he brutally besieged Homs and quelled Syrian uprisings, the gathering Abbasid storm in the east was quietly preparing to sweep away the entire Umayyad order under Ibrahim the Imam and Abu Muslim. This breakdown explores the military maneuvers, palace coups, and deep-seated tribal fractures that defined the climax of the Third Fitna.

recent_video_title: Ibn Qudāmah: Life, Legacy, Khirqah, and Karāmāt
recent_video_description:
Imām Muwaffaq al-Dīn Ibn Qudāmah al-Maqdisī (d. 620 AH) stands among the most influential scholars in the history of the Ḥanbalī school. In this lecture, we explore his life, scholarly formation, and enduring legacy, with particular attention to his journey to Baghdad and his relationship with the celebrated Ḥanbalī scholar and spiritual master, Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī. Drawing from classical biographical sources, we examine Ibn Qudāmah’s personal recollections of studying alongside his cousin, al-Ḥāfiẓ ʿAbd al-Ghanī al-Maqdisī, and the profound influence of their teacher.

Beyond their studies in jurisprudence and ḥadīth, Ibn Qudāmah recounts receiving the khirqah directly from Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir, offering a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between religious knowledge and spiritual practice within the Ḥanbalī tradition. We also explore his testimony concerning the karāmāt attributed to his teacher and the later transmission of the Qādirī path alongside Ḥanbalī jurisprudence. Together, these accounts reveal a scholarly tradition in which the pursuit of knowledge was inseparable from spiritual refinement, devotion, and righteous action.

#সূরাবাকারা #surahbaqarah 


Surah Al-Baqarah سورة البقرة

সূরা বাকারা, কুরআনের সবচেয়ে দীর্ঘতম সূরা, আয়াত সংখ্যা ২৮৬, মাসহাফে এটি সূরা ফাতিহার পর দ্বিতীয় ক্রমে এর অবস্থান। রেওয়ায়েত রয়েছে যে ইহা মদিনায় নাযিল হওয়া সর্বপ্রথম সূরা, তবে এই আয়াতটি ছাড়া وَاتَّقُوا يَوْمًا تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى اللهِ ثُمَّ تُوفَّى كُلُّ نَفْسٍ مَا كَسَبَتْ وَهُمْ لَا يُظْلَمُونَ কেননা, এটি আসমান থেকে নাযিলকৃত শেষ আয়াত যা বিদায় হজ্জের সময় মিনায় কোরবানীর দিন নাযিল হয়েছে। সুদ সংক্রান্ত আয়াতও কুরআনের প্রথম দিকে নাযিল হয়। খালিদ বিন মা'দান বলেন, এ সূরার মর্যাদা, মহিমা, হুকুম-আহকাম ও উপদেশের আধিক্য ইত্যাদি কারণে একে ফুসতাতুল কুরআন (কুরআনের বসতি) বলা হয়। উমর ইবনুল খাত্তাব এ সূরাটির আইনশাস্ত্র এবং এতে যা আছে তা শিখতে বারো বছর সময় নেন, যেখানে তাঁর পুত্র আবদুল্লাহ ইবনে উমর আট বছরেই শিখে ফেলেছিলেন। কারণ এ সূরাটি একেবারে নাযিল না হয়ে ধাপে ধাপে নাযিল হয়।

আবু মাসউদ আল-আনসারী (রাঃ) থেকে বর্ণিত, তিনি বলেন, নবী করীম সাল্লাল্লাহু আলাইহি বলেছেনঃ "সূরা বাকারার শেষের দুটি আয়াত, যে ব্যক্তি রাতে পাঠ করবে, তা তার জন্য যথেষ্ট।" [১২]

আবু হুরায়রা (রাঃ) থেকে বর্ণিত যে, সাল্লাল্লাহু আলাইহি ওয়াসাল্লাম বলেছেনঃ "তোমরা তোমাদের ঘরকে কবর বানাবে না, আর যে ঘরে সূরা বাকারা পাঠ করা হয় সে ঘরে শয়তান প্রবেশ করবে না।" [১৩] [১৪][১৫]

সাহল বিন সাদ (রাঃ) থেকে বর্ণিত, রাসূলুল্লাহ () বলেছেনঃ "প্রত্যেক জিনিসেরই একটি কুঁজ থাকে, এবং কুরআনের কুঁজ হল বাকারা সুরা, আর যে ব্যক্তি এক রাতে নিজের ঘরে এটি পাঠ করবে, শয়তান তার তিন রাত পর্যন্ত প্রবেশ করবে না।" [১৬]

আবু (রা) থেকে বর্ণিত, তিনি বলেন, আমি রাসূলুল্লাহ (সাল্লাল্লাহু 'আলাইহি ওয়া সাল্লাম)-কে বলতে শুনেছি: "তোমরা কোরআন পড়, কেননা কেয়ামতের দিন এটি তার লোকদের জন্য সুপারিশ করবে। তোমরা জাহরাউইন (আল-বাকারা এবং আল-ইমরান) পাঠ কর, কারণ তারা কিয়ামতের দিন আসবে যেন তারা মেঘ বা দুটি মেঘ। অথবা যেন কিয়ামতের দিন তারা দুই দল পাখী তাদের পরিবারের পক্ষে তর্ক করছে। তারপর তিনি বললেন: সুরা বাকারা পড়, কেননা এটা আকড়ে ধরা আশীর্বাদ, আর ছেড়ে দেয়াটা আফসোস। এবং কোনো বাতলাহ ধরতে পারবে না।" [১৭]

জাহরাউইন অর্থ: দুটি আলোক, আল-গিয়াবাহ অর্থ: যা উপর থেকে ছায়া দেয়, আল-ফারাক: কোন কিছুর টুকরো, বাতালাহ অর্থ: যাদুকররা।

ঘটনাটি সূরা আল-বাকারার ৬৭-৭৩ নং আয়াতে উল্লেখ করা হয়েছেঃ

"স্মরণ কর, যখন মূসা (আ.) স্বীয় সম্প্রদায়কে বলেছিল, 'আল্লাহ তোমাদেরকে একটি গরু যবহ করার আদেশ দিচ্ছেন'; তারা বলেছিল, 'তুমি কি আমাদের সঙ্গে ঠাট্টা করছো? মূসা বলল, আল্লাহর আশ্রয় নিচ্ছি, যাতে আমি অজ্ঞদের অন্তর্ভুক্ত না হই।"
তারা বলল, 'আমাদের জন্য তোমার প্রতিপালককে স্পষ্টভাবে জানিয়ে দিতে বল তা কীরূপ? মূসা বলল, 'আল্লাহ বলছেন, তা এমন এক গরু যা বৃদ্ধও নয় এবং অল্প বয়স্কও নয়- মধ্য বয়সী। সুতরাং যা (করতে) আদিষ্ট হয়েছ, তা পালন কর'।"

"তারা বলল, 'তুমি আমাদের জন্য তোমার রবের নিকট দো'আ কর, তিনি যেন আমাদের জন্য স্পষ্ট করে দেন, কেমন তার রঙ'? সে বলল, 'নিশ্চয় তিনি বলছেন, নিশ্চয় তা হবে হলুদ রঙের গাভী, তার রঙ উজ্জ্বল, দর্শকদেরকে যা আনন্দ দেবে'।"

"তারা বলল, 'তুমি আমাদের জন্য তোমার রবের নিকট দো'আ কর, তিনি যেন আমাদের জন্য স্পষ্ট করে দেন, তা কেমন? নিশ্চয় গরুটি আমাদের জন্য সন্দেহপূর্ণ হয়ে গিয়েছে। আর নিশ্চয় আমরা আল্লাহ চাহে তো পথপ্রাপ্ত হব'।"

"সে বলল, 'নিশ্চয় তিনি বলছেন, 'নিশ্চয় তা এমন গাভী, যা ব্যবহৃত হয়নি জমি চাষ করায় আর না ক্ষেতে পানি দেয়ায়। সুস্থ যাতে কোন খুঁত নেই'। তারা বলল, 'এখন তুমি সত্য নিয়ে এসেছ'। অতঃপর তারা তা যবেহ করল অথচ তারা তা করার ছিল না।"

"আর স্মরণ কর, যখন তোমরা একজনকে হত্যা করলে অতঃপর সে ব্যাপারে একে অপরকে দোষারোপ করলে। আর আল্লাহ প্রকাশ করে দিলেন তোমরা যা গোপন করছিলে।"

"অতঃপর আমি বললাম, 'তোমরা তাকে আঘাত কর গাভীটির (গোশতের) কিছু অংশ দিয়ে। এভাবে আল্লাহ জীবিত করেন মৃতদেরকে। আর তিনি তোমাদেরকে তাঁর নিদর্শনসমূহ দেখান,যাতে তোমরা বুঝ।"

সূরা আল-বাকারার এই নামে নামকরণ করা হয়েছে কারণ এতে বনী ইসরাঈলের গাভীর কাহিনী রয়েছে এবং এটি ইহুদীদের কাছ থেকে যেমন ঘটেছিল আল্লাহর আইন বাস্তবায়নের জন্য তাড়াহুড়ো করার প্রয়োজনীয়তা নির্দেশ করে। সূরা আল-বাকারার অন্যতম উদ্দেশ্য হল উম্মতকে পৃথিবী গড়ার জন্য প্রস্তুত করা, আল্লাহর ধর্ম প্রতিষ্ঠা করা এবং মানুষের প্রকৃতি স্পষ্ট করে দেওয়া এবং এতে রয়েছে ইমানের ভিত্তি এবং শরীয়তের সম্পূর্ণতা। [১৮]

সূরা আল-বাকারার সবচেয়ে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ বৈশিষ্ট্যগুলির মধ্যে রয়েছে:

এটি কোরানের দীর্ঘতম সূরা। [১৯]

এতে পবিত্র কোরআনের শেষ আয়াত রয়েছে।

এটি কোরানের দীর্ঘতম আয়াত (ঋণের দায়েনা আয়াত) ধারণ করে।

এতে রয়েছে কোরআনের সর্বশ্রেষ্ঠ আয়াত (আয়াতুল কুরসি)।

নবীর জীবনীতে উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে, এ সূরা কিয়ামতের দিন তার পাঠকের পক্ষে লড়বে, এ সূরাতে রয়েছে ইসমে আজম, তাকে এটি দ্বারা ডাকা হলে তিনি উত্তর দেন এবং এটি আকড়ে ধরা আশীর্বাদ এবং এটি ছেড়ে যাওয়া অনুশোচনা, এবং যাদুকরেরা এটি বহন করতে পারে না।

​Surah Al-Kahf: The Stories of the 4 Trials (Lessons & Spiritual Shield) 🛡️✨

​Why are we commanded to recite Surah Al-Kahf every Friday? Far from just a collection of ancient historical events, this extraordinary surah serves as our weekly shield, map, and spiritual compass. In this deep dive, we explore the four legendary trials of humanity described in Surah Al-Kahf—Faith, Wealth, Knowledge, and Power—and uncover the timeless wisdom we need to survive the greatest tests of this worldly life (and the tribulations of the end of times).

​In this video, we break down each story and the essential cures Allah gives us:

​🕒 Timestamps:

0:00 - Introduction: The Secrets of Surah Al-Kahf

1:15 - Trial 1: Faith — The People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf)

Witness the inspiring story of the young believers who chose isolation over disobedience. Driven out of their homes by a tyrant king for refusing to worship idols, they took refuge in a massive cave. Allah put them to sleep for over 300 years, protecting their faith from a world that mocked everything they stood for. The Cure: Seek righteous companionship and place absolute trust in Allah.

​4:45 - Trial 2: Wealth — The Two Gardens

The cautionary tale of a man blessed with two sprawling, lush, and abundantly fruitful gardens. But as his pride grew, gratitude left his heart. He boasted of his superiority, looked down on others, and forgot the One who gave him everything—until he woke up to find his paradise turned to ashes. The Cure: Stay humble, recognize the true Giver, and practice gratitude.

​8:30 - Trial 3: Knowledge — Musa (AS) & Al-Khidr

Journey alongside Prophet Musa (AS) on his quest to learn from the wise servant Al-Khidr. Guided through seemingly inexplicable and tragic events—a damaged boat, a heartbreaking loss, and an unpaid repair—Musa learns that human understanding is strictly limited, and that Allah's divine wisdom operates far beyond our immediate perception. The Cure: Humility, patience, and trusting the unseen plan of Allah.

​12:15 - Trial 4: Power — Dhul-Qarnayn

Uncover the saga of the righteous, just, and unstoppable ruler Dhul-Qarnayn, who traveled to the ends of the earth. When a desperate people begged for protection from Gog and Magog (Yajuj and Majuj), he refused payment, gathered their labor, and erected an epic barrier of iron and copper. Instead of taking the credit, he proclaimed, "This is a mercy from my Lord." The Cure: Sincerity and using your influence, strength, and resources to serve others.

​✨ The Ultimate Shield: The Prophet ﷺ warned us that whoever memorizes the first ten verses of Surah Al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjal (Anti-Christ). This is because the Dajjal will test humanity with these exact four trials.

​Watch, reflect, and share this reminder to bring the light of Surah Al-Kahf into your week!

recent_video_title: What Makes a Muslim Community Strong?
recent_video_description:
What makes a Muslim community strong?

After spending the summer in Toronto and having the opportunity to speak to different Muslim communities, I found myself returning again and again to the same subject: love.

A community is only as strong as the individuals who make it up. And our real strength lies in each of us having his own personal, meaningful and loving relationship with Allah — a relationship that does not depend upon parents, teachers, organisations or anyone else.

This is especially important when raising our children. We don't merely want them to obey Allah because their parents are watching, or even simply out of fear or the desire for reward. We want them to worship Allah because they love Him.

And sometimes we discover the depth of that relationship in unexpected ways — even through hardship. If a tribulation strikes and the first thought that comes to your heart is, “Is Allah displeased with me?”, then notice something beautiful: the first One your heart turned to was Allah.

As I mention in the video:

“Is there a greater fear than losing the love of the one you love?”

Ultimately, strong families, strong communities and a strong Ummah begin in the same place:

Your own relationship with Allah.

It starts with you.

recent_video_description:
This lecture, delivered by Sheikh Ammar Yasir at Masjid Omar, focuses on the fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence) regarding actions that are considered disliked (makruh) during prayer (salah).

Key topics covered include:

Distractions and fidgeting: The speaker explains the importance of maintaining focus and humility (khushu) in prayer, advising against unnecessary movements or playing with clothing, hair, or surroundings.
Postural discipline: Discussion on maintaining proper composure and avoiding haste, which can detract from the reverence of the act of worship.
Disliked bodily actions: Guidance on specific physical habits or expressions that should be avoided to preserve the sanctity and correctness of the prayer.
The purpose of prayer: A recurring theme is that the prayer is a direct conversation with the Creator, and therefore, one should strive to perform it with the utmost care, stillness, and concentration.
Throughout the session, the Sheikh provides practical advice on how to refine one's prayer by eliminating these minor distractions, emphasizing that perfection in the outward form of prayer helps facilitate deeper spiritual connection.

recent_video_description:
Shaykh Mikaeel on why staying in a broken marriage out of fear of being broke or alone completely misses who Allah is.

Have you ever stayed in a painful situation just because you were terrified of what happens to your security once you leave? You convince yourself that your spouse is the source of your sustenance and love. But Allah reminds you that people are merely channels, not the ultimate source. When you cling out of terror, you forget His name Al-Mughni, The Enricher.

Look at the story of Barira and Mughith in Medina, where the Prophet ﷺ respected her choice to walk away, or how Allah enriched the Prophet ﷺ through Khadija without making her irreplaceable. When a separation happens, the Quran promises that Allah will enrich both people from His boundless abundance. What you need comes directly from Him, never just the human channel.

If you've been terrified to walk away from a toxic marriage because you fear ending up broke or alone, this will reframe your tawakkul.
If you've been struggling to stay patient and avoid haram while waiting for the means to get married, take heart in Allah's timing.
If you've ever felt completely empty while chasing superficial wealth or social media validation, this reminder shows where true richness lives.

If this lecture helped you, share it with someone who needs to hear that Allah is Al-Mughni and can enrich them even through divorce or delayed marriage. May Allah reward you.

Jurong appeared on the map as early as 1828 and probably derived from the Malay word 'Jerong', which means shark. This was a special gathering for the final recitation and completion of this great masterpiece of Imam Malik ibn Anas, followed by the granting of Ijazah with connected chains of transmission under the guidance of His Eminence, Shaykh Muhammad Al-Yaqoubi 

Studying the six major hadith collections with precision, paying attention to the exact wording, the names of the narrators, and the authenticity of the texts, is one of the most essential foundations for students of sacred knowledge. This is the very path that Shaykh al-Yaqoubi continues to uphold, following the way of the great hadith masters and pious scholars of the past.

BIOGRAPHY 

Shaykh Muhammad al-Yaqoubi, a descendent Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a world-renowned Syrian scholar of Islamic jurisprudence, hadith, and theology. He is widely recognised as one of the most influential Muslim leaders in the world; with his speeches, classes, and books having impacted thousands of lives for the better.

A prolific writer and poet, his most recent books - ‘Shama’il of al-Habib al-Mustafa’ and ‘Introduction to Sahih al-Bukhari’ - are indispensable for Muslim learners. He has penned 60 poems, of over 5000 lines, in praise of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ - including the doubling (tashtir) of the famous Burdah and Hamziyya poems - which earned him the title of ‘the Busiri of this time’. 

In recognition of his work for building peace and harmony, and better understanding between all religious groups, Shaykh al-Yaqoubi received the International Award of Ambassador of Liberty and Peace in 2016.

For several years running, the Royal Aal al-Bayt has included him as one of the 500 most influential Muslims in the world, with the 2026 edition placing him 33rd.

His bestselling book, ‘Refuting ISIS’, has been published in 10 languages, including Arabic and English, and is widely heralded by critics. The book has played a significant role in the defeat of the ideology of Daesh and has been accredited with saving the lives of many youths, whilst helping people worldwide understand Islam’s position on this topical issue.

The Shaykh speaks 5 languages and has lectured in 35 countries.

El estudio de las seis colecciones principales de hadices con precisión —prestando atención al texto exacto, a los nombres de los narradores y a la autenticidad de los relatos— es uno de los fundamentos más esenciales para los estudiantes del conocimiento sagrado. Este es precisamente el camino que el Sheij al-Yaqoubi (que Allah le preserve) continúa manteniendo, siguiendo la senda de los grandes maestros del hadiz y de los sabios piadosos del pasado.

Habrá una área separada disponible para las hermanas, desde donde podrán ver y escuchar la recitación. También habrá una sala para madres y bebés, in sha Allāh.

BIOGRAFÍA

El Sheij Muhammad al-Yaqoubi, descendiente del Profeta Muhammad ﷺ, es un erudito sirio de renombre mundial en jurisprudencia islámica, hadiz y teología. Es ampliamente reconocido como uno de los líderes musulmanes más influyentes del mundo; sus discursos, clases y libros han impactado positivamente la vida de miles de personas.

Es un prolífico escritor y poeta. Sus libros más recientes —Shamā’il de al-Habīb al-Mustafā e Introducción a Sahīh al-Bujārī— son indispensables para los estudiantes musulmanes. Ha compuesto 60 poemas, con más de 5.000 versos, en alabanza al Profeta Muhammad ﷺ —incluidos los hemistiquios (tashtīr) de los célebres poemas al-Burda y al-Hamziyyah— lo que le concedió el título de “el Būsīrī de nuestra época”.

En reconocimiento a su labor en favor de la paz, la armonía y un mejor entendimiento entre todos los grupos religiosos, el Sheij al-Yaqoubi recibió en 2016 el Premio Internacional de Embajador de la Libertad y la Paz.

Durante varios años consecutivos, la Casa Real Aal al-Bayt lo ha incluido entre los 500 musulmanes más influyentes del mundo; la edición de 2026 lo sitúa en el puesto 33.

Su libro superventas “Refutando a ISIS” ha sido publicado en 10 idiomas, incluidos el árabe y el inglés, y ha recibido un amplio reconocimiento de la crítica. La obra ha desempeñado un papel significativo en la derrota de la ideología de Daesh y se le atribuye haber salvado la vida de muchos jóvenes, además de ayudar a personas de todo el mundo a comprender la postura del islam sobre este tema contemporáneo.

El Sheij habla 5 idiomas y ha impartido conferencias en 35 países.

recent_video_title: 3 Men Were Given Blessings. Only 1 Passed.
recent_video_description:
In this video, Sheikh Muiz Bukhary journeys through this powerful authentic narration from Al-Bukhārī and Muslim and uncovers a dimension of the story that is frighteningly relevant to our lives today. 

Three men. Three extraordinary transformations. But only one of them understood what was really happening.

The Prophet ﷺ told us the remarkable story of three men from Banī Isrāʾīl: a man afflicted with a severe skin condition, a bald man, and a blind man.

Allah healed them.

Allah gave them wealth.

Allah multiplied what they had until each possessed an entire valley of livestock.

It sounds like the test was over.

But it had only just begun.

Because sometimes the greatest test is not what happens when Allah takes something away from you.

It is what happens to your heart after Allah gives you everything you once desperately wanted.

What happens when yesterday's miracle becomes today's normal?

What happens when the blessing you once begged Allah for becomes something you barely notice?

And if your past walked up to you today, would you even recognize it?

Perhaps the question is not simply whether Allah has blessed you.

The question is:

What have His blessings done to your heart?

وَمَا بِكُم مِّن نِّعْمَةٍ فَمِنَ اللَّهِ

“Whatever blessing you have is from Allah.”
(Qur'an 16:53)


If this reminder benefits you, share it with someone who may need to hear it.

Mufti Saif Al-Asri is a prominent Islamic scholar renowned for his dedication to Islamic education, refined character, and profound knowledge of the Shari'ah sciences. He was born in the city of Hajja, Yemen, before relocating to Saudi Arabia with his family at a young age due to his father's work. In Saudi Arabia, he began his early education, entering the kingdom at the age of four or five. Shaykh Saif completed his elementary studies there and started reading religious books under scholars by 12, showcasing an early commitment to seeking knowledge.

Upon returning to Yemen, his family settled in the capital, Sana’a, where Shaykh Saif began his journey in structured Islamic learning. He pursued his intermediate (known as الإعدادية) and secondary education there, simultaneously embarking on formal Islamic studies under the mentorship of several Yemeni scholars. One of the most influential figures in his education was Shaykh Hasan Muhammad Maqbul Al-Ahdal, under whom Shaykh Saif studied the Arabic language, Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), fundamentals of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), and hadith sciences. During this period, he completed the memorization of the Qur’an, which he had begun in Saudi Arabia.

Shaykh Saif furthered his education by enrolling at Al-Iman University in Sana’a, a prestigious institution focusing on Islamic studies. He was among the university's first students when it opened its doors in the early 1990s (1415 AH). During his time there, he studied under leading Islamic scholars, including the distinguished jurist and legal theorist Shaykh Abdul Karim Zaidan, who authored notable works such as *Al-Mufassal Fi Ahkam Al-Mar’a* and *Al-Wajiz Fi Usul Al-Fiqh*. Shaykh Saif studied several of Shaykh Zaidan’s books in Islamic jurisprudence, legal principles, and da'wah (Islamic propagation).

In addition to Shaykh Zaidan, Shaykh Saif studied with other prominent scholars, such as the Yemeni mufti and judge Muhammad bin Isma’il Al-‘Amrani, the founder of Al-Iman University Shaykh Abdul Majid Al-Zindani, and Shaykh Dr. Abdul Wahhab Al-Daylami, a notable specialist in Qur’anic exegesis. This early foundational education enabled Shaykh Saif to comprehensively understand Shari'ah sciences.

After obtaining his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in 2001, Shaykh Saif began his professional career in Islamic jurisprudence by joining the Islamic advisory team at the Qatar Fatwa Center under IslamWeb, a well-known Islamic network. He served as a mufti from 2001 to 2007, dealing directly with the public's written and oral inquiries, gaining valuable experience in providing Islamic guidance and advisory services. His work involved answering questions via calls, SMS messages, and emails, which enhanced his proficiency in contemporary Islamic issues.

While in Qatar, Shaykh Saif continued his studies under scholars like the renowned scholar of Islamic theology and logic, Shaykh Mustafa Al-Binjawani, and the Iraqi scholar Shaykh As-Sadiq Al-Iraqi. Under their mentorship, he deepened his understanding of logic, rhetoric, and Islamic dialectics.

In 2007, Shaykh Saif moved to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to work in the official Fatwa Center. Over the course of nearly a decade (2007-2016), he expanded his expertise in issuing fatwas, supervising junior muftis, and reviewing religious rulings. His long tenure in Qatar and the UAE fortified his experience in Islamic jurisprudence and broadened his knowledge of contemporary Muslims' diverse issues.

Desiring to further his academic credentials, Shaykh Saif pursued a Ph.D. at Mohammed V University in Rabat, Morocco, under Dr. Farouq Hamada, a prominent Hadith scholar and academic figure. Dr. Hamada, originally from Homs, Syria, is well-regarded for his contributions to Islamic academia and his role in shaping the next generation of scholars.

Shaykh Saif’s scholarly endeavors extended beyond academia and fatwas. He has authored several writings on Islamic jurisprudence, creed, and other areas of Shari’ah, making a valuable contribution to Islamic literature. His commitment to Islamic education and scholarly advancement has led him to travel and teach in various regions, including recent visits to Chechnya. Shaykh Saif's connection with Chechnya began with his participation in educational and religious conferences and has since grown into a long-term commitment to supporting Islamic education there.

In Chechnya, Shaykh Saif has been actively involved in teaching students at Islamic universities and delivering classes on key Islamic texts, including Sharh al-Waraqat in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) and Sharh al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah by Al-Imam Abdul-Ghani Al-Maydani. His classes attract students from the Islamic University in Grozny, and he holds study sessions after the noon prayer and on designated days each week. His approach emphasizes a balance between academic rigor and an emphasis on the ethical dimensions of Islamic teachings.

Pharaoh had just watched Musa (as) perform a miracle. He couldn’t deny what the people saw, so he did something more subtle and effective: he labeled it as magic.  — Why words like “extremism” and “moderation” aren’t neutral, and what they assume

The Qur’an was not revealed simply to be recited beautifully. It was revealed to be understood, reflected upon, and acted upon.

recent_video_title: Piety Is Not Punishment | O You Who Believe Ep. 25 | Mustafa Briggs | Ramadan 2026
recent_video_description:
"O you who believe, do not make unlawful the good things which Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress." (5:87)

Islam is not a religion of extremes.

Allah made beautiful things lawful for you.
Good food. Marriage. Rest. Enjoyment. Comfort.

And then He told you not to forbid them upon yourself.

Because there is a type of person who thinks the closer you get to Allah, the more you must suffer.
Who believes that denying yourself everything is the path to piety.

But that is not what Allah asked.

He asked for balance.
Enjoy what is good. Avoid what is harmful. Do not cross the limits.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) corrected the companions who wanted to pray all night, fast every day, and never marry. He told them that was not his way.

Piety is not punishment.
Worship is not deprivation.
And gratitude for what Allah made lawful is itself an act of faith.

Ramadan teaches us discipline, not denial.
We fast to appreciate, not to suffer.

recent_video_title: Top Mufti at Islamweb.net Makes Jake Brancatella Look Like a Fool
recent_video_description:
Mufti Saif Al-Asri is a prominent Islamic scholar renowned for his dedication to Islamic education, refined character, and profound knowledge of the Shari'ah sciences. He was born in the city of Hajja, Yemen, before relocating to Saudi Arabia with his family at a young age due to his father's work. In Saudi Arabia, he began his early education, entering the kingdom at the age of four or five. Shaykh Saif completed his elementary studies there and started reading religious books under scholars by 12, showcasing an early commitment to seeking knowledge.

Upon returning to Yemen, his family settled in the capital, Sana’a, where Shaykh Saif began his journey in structured Islamic learning. He pursued his intermediate (known as الإعدادية) and secondary education there, simultaneously embarking on formal Islamic studies under the mentorship of several Yemeni scholars. One of the most influential figures in his education was Shaykh Hasan Muhammad Maqbul Al-Ahdal, under whom Shaykh Saif studied the Arabic language, Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), fundamentals of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), and hadith sciences. During this period, he completed the memorization of the Qur’an, which he had begun in Saudi Arabia.

Shaykh Saif furthered his education by enrolling at Al-Iman University in Sana’a, a prestigious institution focusing on Islamic studies. He was among the university's first students when it opened its doors in the early 1990s (1415 AH). During his time there, he studied under leading Islamic scholars, including the distinguished jurist and legal theorist Shaykh Abdul Karim Zaidan, who authored notable works such as *Al-Mufassal Fi Ahkam Al-Mar’a* and *Al-Wajiz Fi Usul Al-Fiqh*. Shaykh Saif studied several of Shaykh Zaidan’s books in Islamic jurisprudence, legal principles, and da'wah (Islamic propagation).

In addition to Shaykh Zaidan, Shaykh Saif studied with other prominent scholars, such as the Yemeni mufti and judge Muhammad bin Isma’il Al-‘Amrani, the founder of Al-Iman University Shaykh Abdul Majid Al-Zindani, and Shaykh Dr. Abdul Wahhab Al-Daylami, a notable specialist in Qur’anic exegesis. This early foundational education enabled Shaykh Saif to comprehensively understand Shari'ah sciences.

After obtaining his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in 2001, Shaykh Saif began his professional career in Islamic jurisprudence by joining the Islamic advisory team at the Qatar Fatwa Center under IslamWeb, a well-known Islamic network. He served as a mufti from 2001 to 2007, dealing directly with the public's written and oral inquiries, gaining valuable experience in providing Islamic guidance and advisory services. His work involved answering questions via calls, SMS messages, and emails, which enhanced his proficiency in contemporary Islamic issues.

While in Qatar, Shaykh Saif continued his studies under scholars like the renowned scholar of Islamic theology and logic, Shaykh Mustafa Al-Binjawani, and the Iraqi scholar Shaykh As-Sadiq Al-Iraqi. Under their mentorship, he deepened his understanding of logic, rhetoric, and Islamic dialectics.

In 2007, Shaykh Saif moved to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to work in the official Fatwa Center. Over the course of nearly a decade (2007-2016), he expanded his expertise in issuing fatwas, supervising junior muftis, and reviewing religious rulings. His long tenure in Qatar and the UAE fortified his experience in Islamic jurisprudence and broadened his knowledge of contemporary Muslims' diverse issues.

Desiring to further his academic credentials, Shaykh Saif pursued a Ph.D. at Mohammed V University in Rabat, Morocco, under Dr. Farouq Hamada, a prominent Hadith scholar and academic figure. Dr. Hamada, originally from Homs, Syria, is well-regarded for his contributions to Islamic academia and his role in shaping the next generation of scholars.

Shaykh Saif’s scholarly endeavors extended beyond academia and fatwas. He has authored several writings on Islamic jurisprudence, creed, and other areas of Shari’ah, making a valuable contribution to Islamic literature. His commitment to Islamic education and scholarly advancement has led him to travel and teach in various regions, including recent visits to Chechnya. Shaykh Saif's connection with Chechnya began with his participation in educational and religious conferences and has since grown into a long-term commitment to supporting Islamic education there.

In Chechnya, Shaykh Saif has been actively involved in teaching students at Islamic universities and delivering classes on key Islamic texts, including Sharh al-Waraqat in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) and Sharh al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah by Al-Imam Abdul-Ghani Al-Maydani. His classes attract students from the Islamic University in Grozny, and he holds study sessions after the noon prayer and on designated days each week. His approach emphasizes a balance between academic rigor and an emphasis on the ethical dimensions of Islamic teachings.

recent_video_title: How to Cope With the Loss of a Spouse
recent_video_description:
How do you recover after losing a spouse while raising children on your own?

In this episode of "Ask Me Anything", I respond to a sister who asked for advice on navigating the loss of her husband and the challenges of single parenting.

Losing a spouse changes your life in ways that take time to process. There is no single way to grieve, and there is no fixed timeline for healing.

In this video, I share some of what helped me and some practical thoughts on moving through grief while continuing to show up for your children.

→ Giving yourself permission to grieve in your own way
→ Finding your own “grieving language”
→ Choosing gratitude for what you had rather than focusing only on what was lost
→ Understanding that grief can soften and change over time
→ Looking after your physical and spiritual wellbeing
→ Maintaining some routine and stability for your children
→ Leaning on family, friends and your community instead of trying to do everything alone
→ Making space for your own needs so you can continue to show up for your children

If you’re going through a loss, I hope this conversation reminds you that you don't have to have everything figured out right away. Healing takes time, and everybody’s journey looks different.

If you have experience of grief or single parenting, share the advice you wish someone had given you in the comments. Your words may help someone else in the community.

In this lecture, Sheikh Nuh Keller examines the growing use of Ozempic (semaglutide), a drug developed for type 2 diabetes but now widely promoted as a weight-loss solution. These dangers show the reductionist error of treating the body as separate parts rather than as an integrated whole.

Sheikh Nuh concludes by pointing to lasting solutions based on balance and discipline, including exercise, strength training, and fasting. As prevention, he stresses the benefit of a daily twelve-hour fasting window and fasting one day each week, practices that preserve health and strengthen resilience.

recent_video_title: 07 The Wajibat of Hajj Explained (Part 2) — Essential Fiqh Every Pilgrim Must Know
recent_video_description:
Understanding the **Wājibāt of Hajj** is essential for every pilgrim who wants their Hajj to be valid, complete, and pleasing to Allah. While many Muslims know the basic rituals of Hajj, fewer understand the difference between the *arkān* (pillars) and the *wājibāt* (obligatory acts), and what happens if one of these obligations is missed. In this detailed and accessible lesson, **Dr Shaykh Omer El‑Hamdoon** explains the Wājibāt of Hajj in a clear, structured, and practical way, helping pilgrims prepare with confidence and clarity.

The Wājibāt are the actions that must be performed during Hajj, and although missing one does not invalidate the entire pilgrimage, it does require a compensatory sacrifice (*dam*). Knowing these rulings before travelling is not simply a matter of technical fiqh — it is part of fulfilling the trust of worship with excellence (*iḥsān*). When a pilgrim understands what Allah has obligated, they walk through the sacred journey with purpose, awareness, and tranquillity.

In this video, **Dr Shaykh Omer El‑Hamdoon** breaks down each Wājib in a way that is easy to follow, supported by evidence from the Sunnah and the understanding of the scholars. Whether you are a first‑time pilgrim or someone revising your knowledge, this lesson will give you the grounding you need to perform Hajj correctly and confidently.

**What you will learn in this video:**  
• The definition of Wājib in the context of Hajj  
• How Wājibāt differ from Arkān and Sunnah acts  
• The list of Wājibāt that every pilgrim must perform  
• The wisdom behind these obligations  
• What to do if a Wājib is missed  
• The rulings related to *dam* (compensatory sacrifice)  
• Practical tips to avoid common mistakes during Hajj  

This lesson is not only for those travelling this year. It is for anyone who wants to deepen their understanding of Islamic jurisprudence, appreciate the structure of Hajj, and recognise how every act — even the technical ones — carries spiritual meaning. The Wājibāt teach discipline, order, humility, and obedience. They remind us that worship is not only about emotion and inspiration, but also about following the guidance of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ with precision and devotion.

**Why this topic matters:**  
Many pilgrims enter Hajj with enthusiasm but without sufficient knowledge. This can lead to confusion, mistakes, or unnecessary hardship. By learning the Wājibāt, a pilgrim protects their worship, avoids doubt, and performs Hajj with a heart that is both sincere and informed. Knowledge brings peace, and clarity brings confidence.

**About the speaker:**  
Dr Shaykh Omer El‑Hamdoon is known for his balanced, clear, and practical approach to Islamic teaching. His ability to combine fiqh, spirituality, and real‑world application makes his lessons accessible to all levels of learners. In this series on the jurisprudence of Hajj, he guides viewers through the essential rulings with precision and warmth.

If this video benefits you, please like, share, and subscribe for more fiqh lessons, spiritual reflections, and educational content. May Allah accept the Hajj of every pilgrim, grant clarity to those preparing, and reward all who seek knowledge for His sake.

recent_video_title: 03. Walking Purposefully Between Safa and Marwa: The Hidden Wisdom of Sa‘i
recent_video_description:
Sa‘i between Ṣafā and Marwah is one of the most powerful journeys within Hajj — a journey that takes only minutes with our feet, but can transform a lifetime within our hearts.

In this video, Dr Shaykh Omer El‑Hamdoon explores the profound spiritual lessons hidden in the footsteps of Hājar (AS), whose courage, trust, and perseverance became immortalised in the rites of Hajj.

Sa‘i is not simply walking or running between two hills. It is a living reminder of a mother’s unwavering faith in Allah at a moment of complete vulnerability. When Hājar ran between Ṣafā and Marwah searching for water for her infant son Ismā‘īl, she embodied the essence of *tawakkul* — taking action with full trust in Allah’s mercy. Her story teaches us that even when we feel alone, unseen, or overwhelmed, Allah is closer than we imagine, preparing relief from places we could never expect.

What does Sa‘i teach us?
It teaches us that effort is not optional. That hope must be active. That trust in Allah is not passive waiting, but striving with the heart and limbs. Sa‘i reminds us that Allah sees every step, every tear, every moment of struggle — and that no sincere effort is ever wasted. The spring of Zamzam did not appear until Hājar had exhausted every possible means. Her perseverance became a symbol for all believers: *Do your part, and Allah will open doors you never knew existed.

In this reflection, Dr Shaykh Omer El‑Hamdoon unpacks the deeper meanings of Sa‘i, showing how this ritual mirrors the emotional and spiritual journeys we all face. Whether you are dealing with hardship, uncertainty, or a test that feels beyond your strength, Sa‘i teaches you how to walk through it with dignity, patience, and trust.

In this video, you will discover: 
• The story of Hājar and the divine wisdom behind her struggle  
• How Sa‘i represents the balance between effort and reliance on Allah  
• Why movement, even when tired, is a form of worship  
• How Sa‘i teaches resilience, hope, and emotional strength  
• The connection between Sa‘i and the believer’s daily challenges  
• Practical ways to apply the lessons of Sa‘i in your personal life  

Sa‘i also teaches us about perspective. From Ṣafā, the path looks long. From Marwah, the return feels tiring. Yet the believer keeps moving — not because the path is easy, but because Allah commanded it. Life mirrors this rhythm: moments of clarity followed by moments of confusion, moments of strength followed by moments of weakness. Sa‘i reminds us that faith is not about never feeling tired — it is about continuing the journey with sincerity.

Why this message matters today: 
In a world filled with anxiety, uncertainty, and constant pressure, the story of Hājar offers a timeless blueprint for spiritual resilience. Her Sa‘i was not just a physical act; it was a declaration of trust in Allah’s plan. Every believer today walks their own Sa‘i — between fear and hope, between difficulty and relief, between effort and surrender. Understanding this ritual can reshape how we face our own struggles.

*About the speaker:*
Dr Shaykh Omer El‑Hamdoon brings together classical Islamic teachings, spiritual reflection, and practical wisdom to help Muslims reconnect with the deeper meanings of worship. His calm, thoughtful style makes complex concepts accessible and spiritually uplifting.

If this video inspires you, please like, share, and subscribe for more reflections, reminders, and spiritually enriching content. May Allah accept the Sa‘i of every pilgrim, ease the struggles of every believer, and fill our hearts with the trust and perseverance of Hājar.  
**Ameen.**

Pharaoh had just watched Musa (as) perform a miracle. He couldn’t deny what the people saw, so he did something more subtle and effective: he labeled it as magic. One word, and the proof became a trick, the messenger became a suspect, and the argument was already tilted before anyone weighed the evidence.

Drawing on the Qur’an’s close attention to names, labels, and accusations, he shows what it looks like to answer without accepting someone else’s frame.

This episode covers:
 — Why words like “extremism” and “moderation” aren’t neutral, and what they assume

recent_video_title: Quranic Dua's for Forgiveness, Safety, Acceptance & Righteous Children | Part 1
recent_video_description:
The Qur’an does not only guide us in belief — it teaches us how to speak to Allah.

In these powerful Qur’anic duʿas, we learn how the Prophets and the righteous asked Allah for forgiveness, safety, acceptance, and righteous generations.

These are not ordinary prayers.
They are words Allah Himself placed in the Qur’an so that we can call upon Him with them.

The first duʿa is the repentance of Adam عليه السلام:

رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَا أَنفُسَنَا وَإِن لَّمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنَا وَتَرْحَمْنَا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْخَاسِرِينَ

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.” (Qur’an 7:23)

This duʿa teaches us the essence of true repentance — no excuses, no blame, just honesty before Allah.

The second duʿa is the prayer of Ibrahim عليه السلام for safety and provision:

رَبِّ ٱجْعَلْ هَٰذَا بَلَدًا ءَامِنًا وَٱرْزُقْ أَهْلَهُۥ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ

“My Lord, make this a secure land and provide its people with fruits.” (Qur’an 2:126)

It reminds us to ask Allah not only for rizq, but also for security, peace, and stability in our homes and communities.

Then comes the beautiful duʿa of Ibrahim and Ismaʿil عليهما السلام while building the Kaʿbah:

رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ

“Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.” (Qur’an 2:127)

Even while doing one of the greatest acts of worship in history, they still feared their deeds might not be accepted.

Finally, they made this powerful duʿa for their children and future generations:

رَبَّنَا وَٱجْعَلْنَا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنَآ أُمَّةً مُّسْلِمَةً لَّكَ

“Our Lord, make us submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to You.” (Qur’an 2:128)

Through these duʿas we learn to ask Allah for:

• sincere repentance
• safety and barakah in our lives
• acceptance of our deeds
• righteous children and generations

May Allah make these duʿas alive in our hearts, accept our repentance, bless our homes, and raise from our families people who truly submit to Him.

Āmīn.

True happiness in the Qur'an and Islamic tradition is tied directly to knowing and purifying the soul (nafs), echoing the famous spiritual axiom often translated as, "He who knows himself knows his Lord". 

The Qur'anic Foundation of Success and Self-Purification
- The Path of Success: The Qur'an explicitly links ultimate well-being and prosperity to self-purification. As stated in Surah Ash-Shams, “Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself.” 
- The Inner State (Sa'adah): In the Qur'an, permanent felicity or happiness (sa'adah) is contrasted with wretchedness on the Day of Judgment, and it belongs to those who find eternal peace in Paradise through God's grace (Qur'an 11:108). 
- The Greatest Bliss: Material accumulations do not define true joy; rather, the ultimate fulfillment is attaining the divine pleasure of Allah. 

Self-Knowledge and Knowing the Creator
- The Axiom: The phrase "He who knows himself is truly happy" was famously highlighted by classical scholars like Imam al-Ghazali in The Alchemy of Happiness, building on the tradition "Man 'arafa nafsahu faqad 'arafa Rabbahu" (He who knows himself knows his Lord). 
- Recognizing Limitations: Scholars explain that acknowledging one's own created weakness, ignorance, and utter dependence leads a person to truly comprehend Allah's infinite strength, knowledge, and absolute glory. 
- Polishing the Heart: Self-knowledge requires stripping away the rust of ego, selfish desires, and earthly illusions so that the inner spiritual heart can reflect divine guidance.

The Great Ḥāfiẓ of Ḥadīth Sayyidunā Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh Part 2 of 2
Delivered by Shaykh Riyadh ul Haq on Friday 17th May 2024 at Al Kawthar Academy, Leicester

FREE audio download: https://soundcloud.com/shaykhriyadhulhaq/great-hafiz-hadith-jabiribnabdillah-part2/

Part 1: https://youtu.be/pwL_9hm9uBQ

This second part deepens the portrayal of Sayyidunā Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh (ra) by focusing on his life of service, simplicity, and deep attachment to the Prophet ﷺ. Through numerous incidents - such as the fulfilment of the Prophet’s promise by Abū Bakr (ra), the Prophet’s personal care during illness, and the well-known miracle of feeding hundreds from a small meal - the talk shows how Jābir’s (ra) life was filled with barakah due to sincerity and devotion. His complete adherence to the Sunnah in even small matters, like eating simple food or walking in battles, reflects a life shaped entirely by imitation of the Prophet ﷺ. His participation in campaigns after Uhud and his eagerness to serve, despite hardship, further highlight his commitment and sincerity.

The talk then shifts into a powerful reflection on the nature of knowledge in Islam. It argues that true ʿilm is not mere information or speech, but a spiritual light embodied through humility, service, and character. Using examples from Jābir’s (ra) life and later scholars, the talk explains how knowledge is transmitted through companionship, respect for teachers, and personal transformation, forming a continuous chain back to the Prophet ﷺ.

The session concludes by warning against modern misunderstandings of knowledge as superficial learning, stressing instead that true scholarship requires immersion in a tradition of sincerity, discipline, and ethical refinement - qualities exemplified by Jābir (ra) and the early generations.
