recent_video_title: Why Are We Not Talking About Sudan?
recent_video_description:
Why do some crises move us deeply — while others barely register?

This talk addresses an uncomfortable but necessary topic: selective compassion. Most people don’t ignore suffering out of malice. Often, it’s because we feel less connected, less familiar, or less represented in the stories we see.

From a psychological perspective, empathy tends to follow familiarity — the people who remind us of ourselves, our families, our culture, or our communities. From an Islamic perspective, however, this becomes a spiritual challenge. Our compassion cannot be based on resemblance alone, but on faith.

Using Sudan as a case study, this lecture explores:

— Why empathy is often selective by nature
— How Islam calls us to expand both our in-group and our compassion
— The meaning of the Ummah being “one body”
— Why some suffering tests our īmān more than others
— How to actively cultivate empathy when it doesn’t come naturally

This is not a message of blame or shaming — but a call to awareness, growth, and action. Islam teaches us that empathy is not only a feeling; it is something we practice, even when it is difficult, unfamiliar, or uncomfortable.

May Allāh expand our hearts to carry the pain of the entire Ummah — not just the parts that feel closest to us.

Islam is not a religion like any other, it’s actually a complete worldview. But what is a worldview? And what does that mean for Muslim uni student?

In this episode of the Firmly Rooted Podcast, we break this down, explaining how phrases Muslim students absorb on campus such as “as long as I don’t harm anyone”, “my body, my choice”, all carry assumptions about reality, knowledge and morality that conflict with it. 

We also touch on the source of doubts - many are driven by emotional and spiritual causes rather than intellectual ones.

We then move onto challenging a victimhood mindset, calling Muslims to treat wider British society as “my people” in the way the prophets did, and to answer global suffering with gratitude, self-reform and principled action.

This video covers:
- What a worldview is, and why everyday phrases like “it’s my choice” are more loaded than they sound
- The wisdom framework: the righteous goal, the context, and applying knowledge in a way that fits, drawn from the example of the Prophet peace be upon him.

recent_video_description:
Are Muslims allowed to vote in America? What does Islam teach about civic participation, justice, and responsibility toward the society in which we live?

In this thought-provoking episode of the SB Life Institute Podcast, host Safraz Bacchus explores an important question facing Muslim communities in the United States: Should Muslims actively participate in the democratic process, and what role does faith play in making that decision?

Drawing on his experiences within the American Muslim community, Safraz discusses the challenges of belonging, anti-Muslim prejudice, political participation, and the importance of recognizing that Muslims are an integral part of the society they call home.

The conversation begins with his experience attending the Muslim Day Parade in New York, where a post promoting unity and togetherness attracted hateful and anti-Muslim comments. He reflects on the importance of responding to prejudice while standing confidently for dignity, belonging, and shared humanity.

### WHAT THIS EPISODE EXPLORES

• Muslims and Voting in America:  Why civic participation matters and how Muslims can exercise their democratic rights.

• Faith and Civic Responsibility:  How Islamic teachings encourage responsibility toward God, family, neighbours, and the wider community.

• The Quran and Justice:  A reflection on Quran 4:135 and the responsibility to stand firmly for justice, even when it is difficult.

• Belonging and Muslim Identity:  Why Muslim Americans should not see themselves as second-class citizens or feel disconnected from their society.

• Choosing Ethical Leadership:  Why integrity, accountability, compassion, and service should matter when evaluating public leadership.

• Empowering the Next Generation: Why young people need education, critical thinking, and opportunities to participate in shaping their communities.

• Unity Over Division:  Why communities benefit from leaders who bring people together rather than divide them based on religion, race, ethnicity, or nationality.

Safraz also discusses the importance of supporting those who work toward justice and the common good, drawing upon the Quranic teaching to cooperate in righteousness and goodness.

This is not about promoting a political party or telling people which candidate to support. It is about understanding civic responsibility, making informed choices, and recognizing the power individuals have to contribute to their communities.

Your voice matters. Your participation matters. And your responsibility toward society does not end at the doors of your home or place of worship.

Prayer Makes Perfect
23rd - 24th February 2013
Weekend Experience

Register Today: http://www.alkauthar.org/course.php?course=373

What do you think of an act of worship -- the most ordered in the Qurʾan, the first on which we'll be judged, the true sign of one's belief, the one that brings you the closest to Allah and the one that brings you to the true station of servitude (prostration)? A simple 5 minute act of worship that is more beloved to Allah than this world and all that is in it!

Little wonder is it not, that the Prophet's last advice before he passed away was: 'The Prayer, the Prayer!'

Yet with such importance, how few are those who learn about it and practice it correctly? On top of that, how much differences exists in the ummah in the manner of prayer? And finally, how pitiful that people don't take the full reward of the prayer -- just as the Prophet (ṣalla'llāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam) said in the authentic ḥadīth: A person prays and yet for him only a tenth or a quarter or a half of its reward is written.

Are you sure your prayers are correct?

Are you sure they are done in the manner that deems them acceptable?

recent_video_description:
Do you want more blessings, peace, and happiness in your life? Do you wish to strengthen your connection with Allah and make Him a part of every moment of your day? The key to a blessed life is not only making dua when you need something, but also remembering Allah consistently throughout your daily routine. In this powerful Islamic reminder, Samih Jad shares six important habits that can help you increase your Dhikr, strengthen your Iman, and develop a deeper relationship with Allah.

The first habit is to take advantage of the blessed times for remembering Allah, especially in the morning after Fajr and in the evening before sunset. These precious moments are excellent opportunities to recite the morning and evening Adhkar taught by Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The second habit is to increase your remembrance of Allah through meaningful words of Dhikr, such as SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah, and Allahu Akbar. Remembering Allah with sincere hearts and understanding the meaning of these beautiful words can bring countless spiritual benefits into your life.

The third habit is to make the recitation of the Holy Quran a part of your daily routine. Even if you begin with a few verses every day, consistency is what matters. Every letter of the Quran carries a reward, and regular recitation helps keep your heart connected to the words of Allah. The fourth habit is to use your free and wasted moments wisely. Whether you are travelling, waiting in a queue, cooking, walking, or completing everyday tasks, you can use these moments to remember Allah instead of allowing your time to pass without benefit.

The fifth habit is to improve your Salah and make it a true opportunity to remember Allah. Prayer should not become a routine performed without concentration or understanding. Instead, give your Salah the attention it deserves, reflect on what you recite, and make sincere Dua to Allah. The sixth and most important habit is to connect Dhikr with every situation in your life, following the beautiful example of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. From waking up and leaving your home to eating, drinking, travelling, experiencing difficulties, and receiving blessings, remember Allah in every situation. You can also speak to Allah in your own language and ask Him for your needs through sincere Dua.

This powerful reminder by Samih Jad teaches us that remembering Allah is not limited to a specific time, place, or form of worship. It is a way of life that keeps our hearts alive and strengthens our connection with our Creator. Start applying these six habits from today, even if you begin with small steps. Make Dhikr a regular part of your daily routine, remain consistent in your worship, and encourage your family and friends to remember Allah as well. May Allah fill our lives with His blessings, grant peace to our hearts, increase our Iman, and make us among those who remember Him abundantly. Ameen.

The Heart or the Brain? Where Does Consciousness Really Reside?

🎥 Presented in 4K with crystal-clear audio

Where does consciousness actually reside? Most people instinctively point to the brain—but is that the only possibility?

For centuries, Muslim scholars have discussed the relationship between the heart, the brain, and the human soul. Today, modern neuroscience and philosophy continue to wrestle with the very same mystery, known as the "hard problem of consciousness."

In this episode of Islam Explained, Shaykh Zakareeya Baksh explores what the Qur'an, Sunnah, and classical Islamic scholarship teach about consciousness. Discover the three major scholarly perspectives on the role of the heart and the brain, why the Qur'an repeatedly describes the heart as a place of understanding, and how these discussions intersect with modern scientific observations.

Rather than reducing the issue to a simple answer, this episode examines the evidence through the lens of revelation and the Islamic scholarly tradition, while engaging with one of the most profound questions in neuroscience and philosophy today.

recent_video_description:
Siraj Wahhaj is an African-American Muslim convert to Islam and public figure for Muslims in North America. He is currently the Imam of Al-Taqwa mosque in Brooklyn, New York and the Amir (Leader) of The Muslim Alliance in North America (MANA).

Born and raised in New York, he became a Sunday school teacher as at a young age, then later went to Wilfrid Laurier University (WLU) where he studied biology education.

In 1969 he joined the Nation of Islam and was taught under Louis Farrakhan at the height of the NOI's anti-Malcolm X rhetoric. He became a Sunni Muslim after the death of Elijah Muhammad in 1975 and Muhammad's son Warith Deen Mohammed took over and reorganized the organization, urging members to come to orthodox Islam. Kearse then changed his name to Siraj Wahhaj. He was chosen to study Islam at the Umm al-Qura university of Mecca in 1978. He also briefly taught a course in Islamic studies at Howard University. In 1981 he started his own mosque, Masijd ul-Taqwa, in a friend's apartment in Brooklyn. Although it originally started out with only 25 people, today it is well-known.

In 1988 he led his community in an anti-drug patrol in which they staked out drug houses in Bedford-Stuyvesant in the cold of winter for 40 days and nights, forcing the closure of 15 drug houses. This effort received high praise from the New York City Police Department and the media.

Since that time, Siraj has been active in many Islamic organizations. He has been vice president of the Islamic Society of North America since 1997 and has served on the Majlis al Shura, a consultative council of Islamic scholars, since 1987. He is a member of the Board of Advisors for the American Muslim Council and has also served on the national board of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

Siraj is a prolific speaker in America. He makes many appearances at major North American Muslim conventions, and numerous forums and lectures in New England. His audio and video lectures are also popular in America's Muslim community. He is known to encourage Muslims to be God-fearing, enjoin good and forbid evil, practice regular charity, stay away from drugs, abstain from pre-marital relations, and other issues as well. He has also appeared on several national television talk shows and has had interviews with several media outlets.

In 1991 Siraj offered an invocation (opening prayer) to the United States House of Representatives. He was the first Muslim to do so.

recent_video_description:
An Israeli company tried to buy his AI startup. He refused. Now, he's taking on ChatGPT, OpenAI, Claude, and Big Tech.

At just 24 years old, Hani Chihabi and his brother built Thaura AI, an alternative to ChatGPT and other major artificial intelligence platforms. Within just two weeks of launching, they reached 100,000 users without spending a penny on advertising.

But what makes someone walk away from a successful career in tech to challenge some of the world's most powerful AI companies? And can we really trust the systems we're increasingly sharing our thoughts, questions, and personal information with?

Born in Syria and raised in Germany, Hani found himself working in the technology industry while watching the destruction unfolding in Palestine. Uncomfortable with the companies and systems he was helping support, he decided to leave his job and build something different.

In this episode of The Thinking Youth, Hani reveals how an Israeli company approached them about acquiring Thaura AI, why they refused to sell, and what it takes to compete against the biggest names in artificial intelligence.

The conversation comes at a particularly important moment for the future of AI.

In an October 19, 2026 interview, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke about the need for greater use of artificial intelligence to counter online narratives and campaigns he accused of influencing young Americans and Europeans against Israel. His remarks highlight a growing debate over the use of AI, bots, and digital platforms to influence public opinion.

As governments and technology giants increasingly recognize AI as a tool of political and economic power, who gets to decide what information we see, what AI systems are allowed to say, and how our conversations and personal data are handled?

With OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and Meta AI becoming increasingly influential, questions surrounding AI censorship, political bias, privacy, surveillance, and the ethics of artificial intelligence are more relevant than ever.

We discuss the darker side of ChatGPT and Big Tech, the politics of artificial intelligence, the risks of centralized AI infrastructure, and why Muslims need to move beyond simply using technology to building their own alternatives.

Hani also shares his remarkable personal journey: teaching himself to code in just seven months, building a company with his brother, reaching 100,000 users, and navigating the personal sacrifices that come with entrepreneurship.

Can we trust ChatGPT with the way we think? Who controls the AI systems shaping our understanding of the world? Can independent AI startups challenge Big Tech? And what would it take to build a genuinely ethical alternative?

This is a conversation about AI, power, privacy, entrepreneurship, faith, and the future of technology.

Genocide doesn't begin with violence alone. It begins with words, dehumanization, propaganda, and the silence of those who witness injustice.

What lessons should we learn from the atrocities of the past and present, and how should those lessons change the way we live?

In this Jumuah khutbah, Shaykh Suleiman Hani explores 7 lessons from genocide and ethnic cleansing, drawing from the Qur'an, the story of the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud), Prophet Musa (AS) and Pharaoh, and examples of oppression throughout history and our world today.

From Palestine and Sudan to Bosnia and the Rohingya, this khutbah examines the patterns of injustice, the responsibilities of witnesses, and the certainty of Allah's justice.

The seven lessons explore:
1. How dehumanization and propaganda pave the way for violence.
2. Why remaining a passive spectator is not always neutral.
3. Why institutions of power cannot be our only source of hope.
4. How oppressors justify their actions and see themselves as righteous.
5. Why no injustice escapes Allah's knowledge or accountability.
6. The importance of breaking cycles of abuse and oppression.
7. Why faith, certainty, and trust in Allah endure beyond oppression.

These lessons aren't limited to global conflicts. They also challenge us to examine how we treat our families, neighbors, colleagues, and communities.

What role do we play when injustice takes place, and what will we leave behind for the next generation?

recent_video_title: Quranic Dua's for Forgiveness, Safety, Acceptance & Righteous Children | Part 1
recent_video_description:
The Qur’an does not only guide us in belief — it teaches us how to speak to Allah.

In these powerful Qur’anic duʿas, we learn how the Prophets and the righteous asked Allah for forgiveness, safety, acceptance, and righteous generations.

These are not ordinary prayers.
They are words Allah Himself placed in the Qur’an so that we can call upon Him with them.

The first duʿa is the repentance of Adam عليه السلام:

رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَا أَنفُسَنَا وَإِن لَّمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنَا وَتَرْحَمْنَا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْخَاسِرِينَ

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.” (Qur’an 7:23)

This duʿa teaches us the essence of true repentance — no excuses, no blame, just honesty before Allah.

The second duʿa is the prayer of Ibrahim عليه السلام for safety and provision:

رَبِّ ٱجْعَلْ هَٰذَا بَلَدًا ءَامِنًا وَٱرْزُقْ أَهْلَهُۥ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ

“My Lord, make this a secure land and provide its people with fruits.” (Qur’an 2:126)

It reminds us to ask Allah not only for rizq, but also for security, peace, and stability in our homes and communities.

Then comes the beautiful duʿa of Ibrahim and Ismaʿil عليهما السلام while building the Kaʿbah:

رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ

“Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.” (Qur’an 2:127)

Even while doing one of the greatest acts of worship in history, they still feared their deeds might not be accepted.

Finally, they made this powerful duʿa for their children and future generations:

رَبَّنَا وَٱجْعَلْنَا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنَآ أُمَّةً مُّسْلِمَةً لَّكَ

“Our Lord, make us submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to You.” (Qur’an 2:128)

Through these duʿas we learn to ask Allah for:

• sincere repentance
• safety and barakah in our lives
• acceptance of our deeds
• righteous children and generations

May Allah make these duʿas alive in our hearts, accept our repentance, bless our homes, and raise from our families people who truly submit to Him.

Āmīn.

How much of who you are today is being shaped by a past you thought you'd left behind?

recent_video_title: Pharaoh’s Strategy Against Musa Is Now a Modern Weapon | Snapshots with Imam Tom Facchine
recent_video_description:
Pharaoh had just watched Musa (as) perform a miracle. He couldn’t deny what the people saw, so he did something more subtle and effective: he labeled it as magic. One word, and the proof became a trick, the messenger became a suspect, and the argument was already tilted before anyone weighed the evidence.

In this Snapshot, Imam Tom Facchine unpacks how that same move still works today, as language frames the moral universe before a debate begins, and why Muslim leaders must learn to recognize when a word or a question is a trap. Drawing on the Qur’an’s close attention to names, labels, and accusations, he shows what it looks like to answer without accepting someone else’s frame.

This episode covers:
 — Why words like “extremism” and “moderation” aren’t neutral, and what they assume
 — Why some questions are built so that answering them means losing, and when a leader should reframe or refuse
 — Four questions to ask of any loaded word before you respond
 — Why Muslims need a moral vocabulary rooted in revelation

Can a child really learn well without going to school every day? In this episode of Uppu Podcast, we sit down with Mariyam and Rustam, founders of Crink, an AI-native online counselling platform, who have homeschooled their four children.

recent_video_title: Artistic Director of San Francisco Ballet Tamara Rojo on choreography, directing, and research
recent_video_description:
What is it really like to leave a 27-year legacy in London to steer one of America’s most historic ballet companies? Three years after her bittersweet departure from the UK, the legendary Tamara Rojo sits down with acclaimed writer and critic Graham Watts for a captivating, wide-ranging conversation. Now fully settled as the Artistic Director of the San Francisco Ballet, Tamara opens up about the relentless pace of her tenure, the staggering structural differences between British and American arts funding, and how she managed to lead the company to a record-breaking $12 million Nutcracker box office. From her refreshing philosophy on respecting historical legacy (rather than letting ego rewrite it) to her pioneering efforts to bring thousands of young, diverse faces into the opera house, Tamara shines as a dynamic, deeply conviction-led force in the global dance community. She also shares fascinating insights into her 6-year PhD research on the psychology of elite dancers, her own celebrated choreography (Raymonda and Cinderella), and what it takes to leave an audience irrevocably changed.

Listen to discover:

Life in California: Tamara reflects on her first three years in San Francisco and what she misses most about the British sense of humour. [03:26]

US vs. UK Arts Funding: The massive shift from relying on a public funding safety net to navigating a system built entirely on box office and multi-generational donors. How a massive, record-breaking anonymous bequest gave her the creative freedom to bridge the old way of running the company with the new. [07:43]

Respecting Legacy Over Ego: Tamara explains her "evolutionary, not revolutionary" approach to leadership and her constructive relationship with predecessor Helgi Tomasson. [13:48]

Diversifying the Audience: Breaking down the perception barriers of ballet and activating the opera house with Mariachi bands, Flamenco, and local community art. [23:15] 

The Psychology of an Elite Dancer: Tamara reveals what she learned from her 6-year "rabbit hole" of PhD research on why some incredibly talented dancers thrive in the studio but struggle on stage. [35:43]

Directing Her Own Choreography: Re-editing Raymonda for American audiences and why her Cinderella has become a staple Christmas tradition in Sweden. [40:20] 

Reflecting on her ENB Legacy: Tamara looks back at her proudest moments at the English National Ballet, from championing female choreographers to securing their state-of-the-art new building. [45:19] 

Interview from the LBC In Conversation series. Recorded on 3rd December 2025.

recent_video_description:
An Israeli company tried to buy his AI startup. He refused. Now, he's taking on ChatGPT, OpenAI, Claude, and Big Tech.

At just 24 years old, Hani Chihabi and his brother built Thaura AI, an alternative to ChatGPT and other major artificial intelligence platforms. Within just two weeks of launching, they reached 100,000 users without spending a penny on advertising.

But what makes someone walk away from a successful career in tech to challenge some of the world's most powerful AI companies? And can we really trust the systems we're increasingly sharing our thoughts, questions, and personal information with?

Born in Syria and raised in Germany, Hani found himself working in the technology industry while watching the destruction unfolding in Palestine. Uncomfortable with the companies and systems he was helping support, he decided to leave his job and build something different.

In this episode of The Thinking Youth, Hani reveals how an Israeli company approached them about acquiring Thaura AI, why they refused to sell, and what it takes to compete against the biggest names in artificial intelligence.

The conversation comes at a particularly important moment for the future of AI.

In an October 19, 2026 interview, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke about the need for greater use of artificial intelligence to counter online narratives and campaigns he accused of influencing young Americans and Europeans against Israel. His remarks highlight a growing debate over the use of AI, bots, and digital platforms to influence public opinion.

As governments and technology giants increasingly recognize AI as a tool of political and economic power, who gets to decide what information we see, what AI systems are allowed to say, and how our conversations and personal data are handled?

With OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and Meta AI becoming increasingly influential, questions surrounding AI censorship, political bias, privacy, surveillance, and the ethics of artificial intelligence are more relevant than ever.

We discuss the darker side of ChatGPT and Big Tech, the politics of artificial intelligence, the risks of centralized AI infrastructure, and why Muslims need to move beyond simply using technology to building their own alternatives.

Hani also shares his remarkable personal journey: teaching himself to code in just seven months, building a company with his brother, reaching 100,000 users, and navigating the personal sacrifices that come with entrepreneurship.

Can we trust ChatGPT with the way we think? Who controls the AI systems shaping our understanding of the world? Can independent AI startups challenge Big Tech? And what would it take to build a genuinely ethical alternative?

This is a conversation about AI, power, privacy, entrepreneurship, faith, and the future of technology.

recent_video_description:
An Israeli company tried to buy his AI startup. He refused. Now, he's taking on ChatGPT, OpenAI, Claude, and Big Tech.

At just 24 years old, Hani Chihabi and his brother built Thaura AI, an alternative to ChatGPT and other major artificial intelligence platforms. Within just two weeks of launching, they reached 100,000 users without spending a penny on advertising.

But what makes someone walk away from a successful career in tech to challenge some of the world's most powerful AI companies? And can we really trust the systems we're increasingly sharing our thoughts, questions, and personal information with?

Born in Syria and raised in Germany, Hani found himself working in the technology industry while watching the destruction unfolding in Palestine. Uncomfortable with the companies and systems he was helping support, he decided to leave his job and build something different.

In this episode of The Thinking Youth, Hani reveals how an Israeli company approached them about acquiring Thaura AI, why they refused to sell, and what it takes to compete against the biggest names in artificial intelligence.

The conversation comes at a particularly important moment for the future of AI.

In an October 19, 2026 interview, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke about the need for greater use of artificial intelligence to counter online narratives and campaigns he accused of influencing young Americans and Europeans against Israel. His remarks highlight a growing debate over the use of AI, bots, and digital platforms to influence public opinion.

As governments and technology giants increasingly recognize AI as a tool of political and economic power, who gets to decide what information we see, what AI systems are allowed to say, and how our conversations and personal data are handled?

With OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and Meta AI becoming increasingly influential, questions surrounding AI censorship, political bias, privacy, surveillance, and the ethics of artificial intelligence are more relevant than ever.

We discuss the darker side of ChatGPT and Big Tech, the politics of artificial intelligence, the risks of centralized AI infrastructure, and why Muslims need to move beyond simply using technology to building their own alternatives.

Hani also shares his remarkable personal journey: teaching himself to code in just seven months, building a company with his brother, reaching 100,000 users, and navigating the personal sacrifices that come with entrepreneurship.

Can we trust ChatGPT with the way we think? Who controls the AI systems shaping our understanding of the world? Can independent AI startups challenge Big Tech? And what would it take to build a genuinely ethical alternative?

recent_video_description: "Islamic history has one of the most remarkable legacies of famous women in human history. This set is primarily biographical and focuses on a select number of prominent women in Islamic history from the Age of the Prophet until modern times in a wide variety of areas from scholarship, mysticism, and poetry to social patronage, war, and politics. It shows that the status of women in Islamic societies has never been uniform or monolithic but has shifted from place to place, from age to age, and from class to social class. The greatest disparity, however, has been between the norms of the Prophetic period and those of subsequent ages. Prophetic society lacked the rigid divisions of social space that became characteristic of many traditional Islam societies, and, as a rule, Prophetic society was more open and less patriarchal, giving women greater freedom and allowing the a conspicuous role within the matrix of social and civic life. A second major shift in women's status occurred during the colonial, post-colonial, and modern periods, when the position of Muslim women often deteriorated markedly. Although the class focuses on the legacies or particular women, it will look at their lives as an index of a number of concrete theological and legal issues pertaining to gender and sexuality in Islam Law and Muslim culture. This set is not intended for women alone or just for Muslims."

recent_video_title: Finding Humans in the Machine Age
recent_video_description:
Since the industrial revolutions of the late nineteenth century, our civilization has increasingly modeled itself after the factory and the processor. We have constructed a world obsessed with raw efficiency, instrumentation, speed, and continuous measurement. In this system, those who learn to think, work, and act like machines are rewarded with status and wealth.



 



Meanwhile, those who long for a more soulful, unhurried existence, seeking to live as integrated human beings connected to the earth, the cosmos, and their Creator, are often sidelined and told to adapt or be left behind. In today’s episode we explore how to reclaim our humanity from the gears of this mechanical age.



 



 



Book recommendations:



 



The Burnout Society by Byung-Chul Han



Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury



 



About the hosts:



Walead Mosaad is an internationally recognized scholar in Islamic studies and human development. His academic and traditional training has accorded him the opportunity to work with communities worldwide as a teacher and project driver. He has completed degrees from Rutgers University and Fath Islamic Seminary in Damascus. He received his PhD from the University of Exeter in Arab and Islamic Studies, and was also classically trained at the Al-Azhar University.



He is currently the Chair and Scholar-in-Residence of Sabeel Community. He has traveled extensively throughout the Muslim world, as well as Europe and the Far East, delivering lectures on various topics, including spirituality, ethics and intercultural peace building.



https://www.sabeelcommunity.org/walead-mohammed-mosaad  



 



 



Rehan Khan is a professor of leadership and novelist. He is an advocate for virtue-based storytelling as well as leading with a moral lens. Over 30 years Rehan has advised several global and regional brands. As an adjunct professor he teaches post-graduate courses in AI and the Future of Work, as well as Leadership: A Moral Perspective, and Personal Influence at one of the world’s leading international business schools.



He is a keen observer of history and techno-science. Rehan is the author of a Tomb of Empires (2024) a historical fiction set in 90BC in the Middle East, the Carnegie nominated A Tudor Turk trilogy (2019-2022) set in the Ottoman Empire and Tudor England, and the fantasy sci-fi series, Tales of Khayaal (2025) set on the Earth like planet of Ikleel. recent_video_title: Pharaoh’s Strategy Against Musa Is Now a Modern Weapon | Snapshots with Imam Tom Facchine
recent_video_description:
Pharaoh had just watched Musa (as) perform a miracle. He couldn’t deny what the people saw, so he did something more subtle and effective: he labeled it as magic. One word, and the proof became a trick, the messenger became a suspect, and the argument was already tilted before anyone weighed the evidence.

In this Snapshot, Imam Tom Facchine unpacks how that same move still works today, as language frames the moral universe before a debate begins, and why Muslim leaders must learn to recognize when a word or a question is a trap. Drawing on the Qur’an’s close attention to names, labels, and accusations, he shows what it looks like to answer without accepting someone else’s frame.

This episode covers:
 — Why words like “extremism” and “moderation” aren’t neutral, and what they assume
 — Why some questions are built so that answering them means losing, and when a leader should reframe or refuse
 — Four questions to ask of any loaded word before you respond
 — Why Muslims need a moral vocabulary rooted in revelation

إذا ما قال لي ربي .. أما استحييت تعصيني
وتخفي الذنب عن خلقي .. وبالعصيان تأتيني
If my Lord asks me
"Have you no shame in disobeying me?
You hide your faults from my creation
yet full of sin you come to Me"

فكيف أجيب يا ويحي .. ومن ذا سوف يحميني
So what will I answer? O' Woe to me,
and who shall protect me do you see?

أسلي النفس بالآمال .. من حين إلى حين
I keep forestalling my soul
with thoughts of hope from time to time

وأنسى ما وراء الموت .. ماذا بعد تكفيني
And forgetting what is to come after death,
and after I am warped in the sheets of the dead

كاني قد ضمنت العيش .. ليس الموت يأتيني
As if I have guaranteed living forever,
and that death will not overcome me

وجاءت سكرة الموت الشديدة من سيحميني
Then the harsh drunkenness of death overtakes me,
who now will be able to protect me?

نظرت إلى الوجوه أليس منهم من سيفديني
I looked at the faces, is there not from amongst them
who will ransom me?

سأسأل ما الذي قدمت في دنياي ينجيني
I will be asked
what have I put forth in my life to save myself

فكيف إجابتي من بعد ما فرطت في ديني
So what will I answer,
after I've been neglectful regarding my Deen

ويا ويحي ألم أسمع كلام الله يدعوني
O' woe to me, did I not hear the
Speech of Allah calling out to me??

ألم أسمع لما قد جاء في ق و يس
Did I not hear what has come in Qaaf'n, wa Yaseen'i

ألم أسمع بيوم الحشر يوم الجمع والدين
Did i not hear of the day the crowds will be summoned,
the day we will be collected, and the day of al-Deen'i

ألم أسمع منادي الموت يدعوني يناديني
Did I not hear the caller of death
calling me; seeking me

فيا رباه عبد تائب من ذا سيؤويه
O my lord a slave to you I come repenting,
who than shall grant me shelter?

سوى رب غفور واسع للحق يهديني
Other than an oft-forgiving Lord,
to the truth he will guide me

أتيت إليك فارحمني وثقل في موازيني
I have come to you, so have mercy on me,
and make heavy my weights

وخفف في جزائي أنت أرجى من يجازيني
And lighten my reckoning you are the best
of who will bring me to reckoning

recent_video_title: Omar Suleiman _ If You Notice These 3 Signs, You’re Among ALLAH's Most Valued Believers
recent_video_description:
Omar Suleiman _ If You Notice These 3 Signs, You’re Among ALLAH's Most Valued Believers
Imam Omar Suleiman is among the most influential Muslim scholars and public intellectuals in the modern era. As an imam, educator, author, activist, and founder of Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research, he has carved out a unique role that bridges classical Islamic tradition and contemporary intellectual discourse. Known for his warm delivery, spiritual depth, and commitment to justice, Suleiman has become a household name among Muslims in North America and beyond. His books, lectures, and online content reach millions worldwide, and his social activism has earned him respect from both Muslim and non-Muslim communities.

This biography aims to provide a comprehensive 4000-word exploration of his life, works, ideas, and legacy. It will cover his early life, religious training, academic achievements, community leadership, intellectual contributions, publications, activism, and his impact on shaping Muslim identity in the West.
Omar Suleiman was born on June 3, 1986, in New Orleans, Louisiana, United States. He grew up in a family of Palestinian descent, one of many immigrant families who carried with them a strong cultural and religious heritage. His parents emphasized both education and faith, instilling in him a sense of devotion to Islam alongside the responsibility of engaging with the wider world.

Growing up in New Orleans, a city marked by cultural diversity, music, and a vibrant mix of communities, Suleiman was exposed early on to pluralism. However, being a Muslim child in post–Gulf War and later post-9/11 America also meant facing identity struggles and questions about belonging. These experiences later informed his commitment to interfaith dialogue and social justice advocacy.

From a young age, he was drawn toward the Qur’an, spirituality, and stories of the Prophets. His religious curiosity was nurtured by his local Muslim community and early mentors. At the same time, his American upbringing exposed him to issues of racism, inequality, and justice — themes that would later feature prominently in his work.
Omar Suleiman pursued a dual path of education — excelling in both secular academia and Islamic studies. He earned bachelor’s degrees in Accounting and Islamic Law, followed by master’s degrees in Islamic Finance and Political History. His intellectual interests ranged from Shariah sciences to modern economics, reflecting his desire to integrate faith with contemporary realities.

Advanced Islamic Studies

He studied under renowned scholars in the United States and abroad, focusing on Hadith, Fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence), Tafsir (Qur’anic exegesis), and theology. His mentors included scholars from diverse traditions of Sunni Islam, giving him a balanced and inclusive perspective.

In 2020, he completed a Ph.D. in Islamic Thought and Civilization at the International Islamic University of Malaysia (IIUM), one of the leading centers of Islamic scholarship in the modern world. His doctoral research deepened his understanding of Islamic intellectual heritage and its application to contemporary challenges.
After completing much of his training, Omar Suleiman returned to serve as an imam in his hometown of New Orleans. He was appointed imam of the Jefferson Muslim Association, where he served for six years.

During this period, he became deeply involved in community service and interfaith work. The devastating impact of Hurricane Katrina (2005) marked a turning point in his life. Alongside other Muslim leaders, he launched initiatives under Muslims for Humanity, providing relief to victims regardless of faith. His leadership during this crisis drew admiration and demonstrated his philosophy of Islam as a force for compassion and public service.

He also co-founded the East Jefferson Interfaith Clergy Association, fostering dialogue among Christian, Jewish, and Muslim communities. His efforts earned him the Outstanding Citizen Award in 2010, a recognition of his ability to bridge faith and civic responsibility.
Later, Omar Suleiman moved to Dallas, Texas, a city with a large and diverse Muslim population. There, he became the Resident Scholar at Valley Ranch Islamic Center. His role included delivering sermons, teaching classes, mentoring youth, and engaging in community activism.

Dallas provided a larger platform for his work. He became co-chair of Faith Forward Dallas at Thanks-Giving Square, a multifaith coalition addressing issues like poverty, racism, and injustice. His reputation as both a spiritual guide and an activist grew significantly during this time.

What if helping others is actually the greatest thing you can do for yourself?

In this powerful reminder, Yasmin Mogahed explains a profound Islamic principle: the way we treat Allah's creation is connected to how we receive His mercy.

When you help someone in need, show mercy to others, forgive those who hurt you, or give something for the sake of Allah, you are not truly losing anything.

You are investing in your Hereafter.

Through powerful reminders from the Quran and Sunnah, Yasmin Mogahed explores:

- Why helping others is ultimately helping yourself
- How Allah promises mercy to those who show mercy
- Why charity is never truly lost
- The reality of what we take with us into the grave
- The power of Sadaqah Jariyah
- How forgiving others can become a means of receiving Allah's forgiveness
- Why everything we give for the sake of Allah remains with us
- The importance of standing against injustice and helping the vulnerable

One of the most powerful lessons in this talk is that what we hold onto in this life will eventually pass away. But what we give for the sake of Allah is never truly lost.

May Allah make us among those who show mercy, forgive others, help those in need, and seek His forgiveness.

Watch until the end and reflect on this question:

**What are you holding onto that Allah is asking you to give?**

Years ago, Khadijah Dawah & Community Services opened its doors through the mercy of Allah and the generosity of a widow who turned her late husband’s empty home into a refuge for women and children in need. It became a place of safety, warmth, and sisterhood — a home for those with nowhere else to go. A little over a year ago, tragedy struck when a fire forced everyone out. Alhamdulillah, with community support, the house was repaired and reopened. But just as the families began to settle back in, another disaster hit: the pipes burst, flooding the crawlspace and neighboring homes. The city had no choice but to shut off the water and close the shelter until repairs could be completed.We found a contractor ready to begin the work. Permits were pulled, and a $3,000 deposit was paid from what little funds remained. Families were moved again — some sleeping in cars, others crowded into a small apartment, and a few staying in a storeroom behind a storefront. So far, $1,500 has been raised, but $12,000 is urgently needed to finish the plumbing and reopen the shelter. Every dollar helps bring women and children back to safety.Every donation helps restore a home built on compassion and faith.
